sources.text:
Meta must pay New Mexico $25 billion for misleading users
(CNN)– Meta has been ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
Wednesday, October 21’s ruling marks one of the largest-ever legal penalties for a tech giant.
In 2018, the company then known as Facebook announced Cambridge Analytica obtained private information of as many as 87 million users.
That information was then used to target voters in the 2016 presidential election.
New Mexico sued, accusing the company of misleading users about its privacy policies and mishandling users’ personal information.

sources.news_title: Meta Ordered to Pay $25 Billion Fine
sources.text:
A judge in New Mexico has ordered Meta to pay a $25 billion fine following a trial that found the company had been lying about Facebook user data for years. Meta is forced to pay its largest fine ever for its deceptive business practices, but it’s just a fraction of the nearly $220 billion warranted under the law. The case stemmed from the Cambridge Analytica scandal over which New Mexico sued Meta in 2021. New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said, “This case has always been about more than one company or one scandal. It is about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences.”

sources.news_title: Meta hit with $25B fine in New Mexico
sources.text:
The 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal was one of the largest user data breaches in history and its repercussions for Meta are still felt to this day. Following a two-week trial, a jury in the State District Court in Santa Fe ruled that Meta had committed 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws.
Each violation was assessed to carry up to $5,000 in penalty charges, leading to the $25 billion fine that Meta is now ordered to pay the state of New Mexico. This is the largest fine against the company to date. To put that number into perspective, Meta made an estimated $42.6 billion in profit through the first half of 2026. The $25 billion fine would eat up nearly 60% of that profit.
Meta was found guilty of deceiving users by allowing third-party app developers to access personal information without their consent. As expected, Meta already confirmed it will appeal the court ruling, with Meta chief legal officer C. J. Mahoney confident that his company will win the appeal.
Earlier this year, New Mexico fined Meta $375 million over violating state practices concerning online child safety.

sources.news_title: Meta whines New Mexico is “impossible” to please after historic $25 billion fine
sources.text:
In his opinion Wednesday, US district court judge Francis J. Mathew said there was no “bright line rule” for determining the appropriate penalty for Meta’s repeated and willful deception of users since 2010 about their “control of data, third-party data misuse, misinformation, hate speech, and equal enforcement.”
New Mexico had asked the court to impose even higher fines, up to $40 billion. The entire state of 2 million people were harmed by Meta’s conduct, Torrez argued, and it seemed dubious that Meta would make meaningful changes unless the penalty impacted Meta’s stock price.
Mathew found that the trial record—which showed that top leadership, including Mark Zuckerberg, were aware that the company, then known as Facebook, was making misleading public representations—supported “the highest level of penalty allowed by the NW Unfair Practices Act.”
“The jury was unequivocal: Facebook systematically misled the public” and “took advantage of the public’s lack of knowledge respecting Facebook’s practices to a grossly unfair degree,” Mathew wrote.
To Mathew, it seemed that Meta made a choice to avoid transparency with users in a bid to capitalize on data they didn’t realize they were sharing and better compete with one of its main rivals, the platform then known as Twitter.
“The violations the jury found were not the product of a single misleading statement or isolated incident,” Mathew noted. “They arose from repeated public representations over more than 11 years, concerning multiple core aspects of Facebook’s platform and business.”
Meta had hoped that New Mexico’s penalty would be more in line with a $5 billion settlement the company made with the Federal Trade Commission to address the Cambridge Analytica fallout. At most, they expected to pay $3.4 billion, while arguing that anything more would be “unconstitutional,” AP News reported.
But Mathew said that the FTC settlement “cannot be viewed in a vacuum” while noting that so far, “penalties, consent agreements, and decrees have not deterred Meta from using deceptive trade practices” since the Cambridge Analytica scandal was first exposed.
“To induce users to provide their personal information to Facebook, Facebook made many false promises respecting the security and control of that data over the course of more than a decade,” Mathew wrote.
Meta will appeal
In a press release, Torrez celebrated the ruling, calling it “a historic day for New Mexico and for consumers across the country.”
“For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law,” Torrez said. “A New Mexico jury found nearly 44 million violations of our consumer protection statute, and this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences. We took on one of the largest companies in the world because New Mexicans deserve honesty, accountability, and the protection of their personal information. Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable.”
A Meta spokesperson confirmed to Ars that the company plans to appeal. Legal experts told Reuters the company has a decent chance at slashing the fine on appeal based on constitutional claims. On top of likely claiming that the penalty is unconstitutional, Meta also feels that “this ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” the spokesperson said.
The eye-popping fine following the multistate settlement appears to be making the company uncomfortable, despite critics claims that New Mexico’s penalty is just a “drop in the bucket” for a company that makes $200 billion annually. On Thursday, the Verge highlighted Meta’s third-quarter earnings report, which showed the company paid close to $10 billion for the multistate settlement. Without that expense, Meta’s income from operations would have been $22 billion higher, the report said.
The excessive penalties come as Meta attempts to reboot its struggling AI strategy, and Meta appeared to signal to Donald Trump’s administration to possibly support its appeal by nodding to its AI wing in its statement opposing the ruling.
“At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online,” Meta’s spokesperson said. “We are confident we will prevail on appeal. In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge.”
AGs warned to keep watch on Meta AI
Nidhi Hegde, executive director of a watchdog nonprofit called the American Economic Liberties Project, told AP News that Meta users want more enforcers willing to take the company to trial rather than settle matters in ways that the FTC settlement suggested weren’t genuine.
In his opinion, Mathew noted that the jury found that Meta internal messages and investigation results showed that “rather than seek to educate Facebook’s users… Zuckerberg chose instead to capitalize on that lack of understanding in order to manipulate users into sharing more of their personal information publicly.” In one message, Zuckerberg was found laying out a plan to deceive users, saying, “Give them a chance to change their privacy settings but obviously don’t encourage it.”
The company also failed to notify users when apps misused their data, only flagging two of 2,000 unique apps associated with data misuse, Mathew said. Following its investigation, Meta’s “decision was deliberately made to narrow Facebook’s internal definition of data misuse so that Facebook would not have to notify as many people due to the operational burden of doing so,” he wrote.
Additionally, Facebook continued knowingly profiting off of pages with misinformation and hate speech, Mathew wrote. Internal research found “substantial amounts of misleading, false, and possibly false political, health, and science content,” with Meta documenting a “greater concentration of false content in top performing advertising content than in top performing Facebook content.”
Rather than share that research, Meta buried it, while also deceiving users in dozens of other ways, including by misrepresenting that the average Facebook users gets “equal treatment” to celebrities and influencers. While Meta claimed everyone was treated the same, one class of users received warning to remove violating content before strikes were applied and frequently got harmful or sketchy content decisions overturned in cases where most users would not.
Hegde told AP News that she thinks as Meta and other company’s AI products grow more popular, it will be increasingly important for states to remain watchful and protect residents from unknown harms.
“Right now, they are rolling out Muse, an AI assistant encouraging people to trust it with everything from their bank accounts to their medical information,” Hegde said. “Which is why we need more enforcers with courage and laws with actual teeth to rein them in.”
Torrez vowed to keep watch in New Mexico and to continue using the blueprint from the Meta case to enforce consumer protection laws and prevent tech giants’ misuse of data.
“This case has always been about more than one company or one scandal,”Torrez said. “It is about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences. New Mexico stood its ground, took this case to trial, and secured a verdict establishing millions of violations of our law. This outcome reinforces a fundamental principle, companies that do business in our state must follow our laws and respect the rights of our people.”
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

sources.news_title: Meta hit with $25 billion penalty over Facebook privacy violations
sources.text:
New Mexico District Judge Francis Mathew has ordered Meta Platforms to pay $25 billion in civil penalties to the state after a court ruled that Facebook misled users about how it handled their personal information and protected their privacy.
The Oct. 21 ruling followed a September jury verdict that found nearly 44 million violations of the state’s Unfair Practices Act in a lawsuit filed by the state in 2021. The penalty ranks among the largest financial penalties imposed on a company in U.S. history, although the amount could be a fraction of Meta’s financial resources. The case stems from the Cambridge Analytica scandal that came to light in 2018.
The scandal raised concerns about the misuse of Facebook users’ personal data for political purposes. The political consulting firm obtained information from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party personality quiz app called “thisisyourdigitallife.” The data was used for political profiling and targeted advertising during the 2016 presidential election campaign.

“Facebook’s wrongdoing – over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public – goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Judge Mathew wrote in his order.
The ruling also addressed the company’s public statements about content moderation, misinformation and hate speech. Under state law, the maximum penalty of $5,000 for each violation could have resulted in a total of approximately $219.5 billion. However, the judge reduced the penalty to $25 billion.
New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez welcomed the judgment, describing it as a landmark victory for consumers. He said the ruling “should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley.”
Meta Platforms plans to appeal the verdict. C.J. Mahoney, the company’s chief legal officer, said in a statement that the lawsuit sought to “impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.”
“We are confident that we will prevail on appeal. In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge,” Mahoney said.

“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” he added.
Meta also agreed to pay $725 million in a 2022 settlement to resolve a class-action lawsuit related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
In a separate case involving alleged harm to teenagers, a jury in March ordered Meta to pay $375 million in penalties. In August, the court ordered the company to pay an additional $567 million into a fund intended to address mental health harms among teenagers who use its platforms. The judge also ordered changes to Facebook and Instagram to better protect children’s well-being.
Meta has appealed the decisions, disputing the court’s findings. The case remains ongoing. The company is also facing multiple similar lawsuits alongside other social media companies, including Snap Inc. and Google.

sources.news_title: New Mexico Judge Orders Meta To Pay $25 Billion in Cambridge Analytica Case
sources.text:
A New Mexico judge has ordered Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties over its handling of the Cambridge Analytica data scandal, according to a court filing issued Wednesday.
CNBC reports that New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew signed the filing on October 21, closing out a legal fight that traces back to 2018, when it first came out that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica had accessed data belonging to 87 million users. The incident predated the company’s rebranding from Facebook to Meta.
A jury in Santa Fe found Meta liable in September for misleading New Mexico residents about how it collected and safeguarded their data and how it prevented harmful information from spreading. Jurors counted more than 43 million violations of the state’s Unfair Practices Act, each carrying a possible civil penalty of up to $5,000. That math initially produced a $219.5 billion award, which Judge Mathew scaled back to $25 billion. Interest will accrue on the unpaid balance at 15 percent a year until Meta settles the debt in full.
In his filing, Mathew wrote that “the extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook’s repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act – $5,000 per violation found by the jury.”
He was just as harsh about how Facebook investigated itself after the Cambridge Analytica revelations broke. Facebook “did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised,” he wrote, pointing to “pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations.” He called the company’s internal examination “willfully ineffective.”
Soros-backed New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez, who oversaw the trial, framed the ruling as a warning to the tech industry. “For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law,” Torrez said, adding that “this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences.”
According to a source who shared their knowledge of the trial with Breitbart News, Torrez and his team included anti-Trump politics at multiple points in the trial. For example, New Mexico’s opening and closing statements reference the end of Meta’s third-party fact checking operation, notorious for censorship conservatives, saying: “because nobody likes being fact-checked, particularly people in power, when Donald Trump ascends to the presidency again, Facebook announces ‘we’re getting rid of third-party fact-checking program,'” sarcastically adding, “that was just a coincidence.”
Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney pushed back hard and signaled an appeal is coming. In a statement provided to Breitbart News, he wrote:
This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico. At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal. In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge.
Numerous conservatives have criticized the New Mexico verdict. Christian First Amendment attorney and head of the American Center for Law and Justice (ACLJ) Jordan Sekulow pointed out that New Mexico is imposing censorship at the threat of massive penalties.
CNN pundit Scott Jennings views the entire trial as revenge for the 2016 election of President Trump:
Conservative influencer ALX points out that leftists want to return to “independent fact checking” because of the dominance of far-left organizations adding fact checks to posts on Facebook.

A New Mexico Judge Just Hit Meta With a $25 Billion Penalty

A New Mexico Judge Just Hit Meta With a $25 Billion Penalty
A New Mexico judge just handed Meta a penalty that dwarfs the FTC's landmark 2019 fine, and the ruling names Zuckerberg and Sandberg personally while targeting conduct the judge called central to Facebook's entire business model.
On Wednesday, October 21, 2026, Judge Francis Mathew of New Mexico’s First Judicial District in Santa Fe ordered Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META | META Price Prediction) to pay the state $25 billion for misleading Facebook users about their privacy in the Cambridge Analytica case. The order is far larger than the $5 billion fine the Federal Trade Commission imposed in 2019 over the same scandal.
The company is appealing. Meta has paid nothing; the money stays tied up, and interest keeps accruing until the appeal is decided.
Shares rose about 2% to $707.81 in afternoon trading after the ruling but faded to close at $697.52, up 0.47%. Third-quarter earnings, not the ruling, drove the after-hours gain of 2.16% to $712.61. The question is whether growing legal bills change the case for a company still growing revenue 26%.
How 43 Million Violations Became a $25 Billion Order
On September 25, jurors found 26 of 29 statements by the company and its leaders misleading. They counted each statement once for every Facebook user or New Mexico resident who saw it, which produced more than 43 million violations of state consumer protection law.
State law allows up to $5,000 per violation. Mathew found more than $219 billion justified but cut it, and all of the money goes to New Mexico schools.
At the October 1 hearing, state lawyer Randi McGinn asked for $35 billion to $40 billion, saying, “This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money.” Meta Platforms asked for a $3.45 billion cap, arguing the state never proved any consumer was misled. The judge’s number is much closer to the state’s request.
Why “Core Business Practices” Raises the Stakes
Mathew wrote that the conduct “goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices” and that “Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false.” He found that the company’s “most senior leadership,” including CEO Mark Zuckerberg and former COO Sheryl Sandberg, misrepresented its data privacy practices.
That language links the finding to the business model and to the top executives. An appeals court will have a harder time narrowing it, and lawyers in other states can cite it in their own cases.
Chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney said Meta is “confident we will prevail on appeal.” Attorney General Raúl Torrez called it “one of the largest, if not the single largest state verdict against a company in American history.”
Legal Costs Are Becoming a Recurring Expense
Torrez sued in 2021 after Cambridge Analytica collected data from as many as 87 million users. Earlier in 2026, New Mexico won $942 million from Meta in two trials over child exploitation and safety claims.
Meta’s third quarter also included a $9.89 billion charge for a separate matter: the August agreement with 52 attorneys general over teen mental health, which provides for payments of up to about $18.59 billion. The New Mexico ruling came after the quarter closed, and Meta has not said whether or when it will book the charge.
The penalty equals about 2.5 times third-quarter net income of $9.86 billion. D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria said, “Meta is worth nearly two trillion dollars, and will likely continue to appeal these cases and drag them out.”
What the $25 Billion Order Means for META Stock
The legal costs look manageable for Meta because third-quarter revenue reached $64.60 billion, and a company with an after-hours market value of about $1.78 trillion can absorb a $25 billion order that is still under appeal.
The risk is that the cases keep multiplying and legal costs permanently reduce margins. Even so, an ad business growing that fast can pay those bills.
Check Meta’s next quarterly filing for any money set aside for New Mexico, and watch whether shares close below $658.49, where they started 2026. A close under that level would mean investors see legal costs as more than a routine expense, and this view would be wrong.

sources.text:
NEW MEXICO (AP) — A judge on Wednesday ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant.

Facebook’s deception was intentional and executives consistently misled users about how the platform worked, state District Court Judge Francis J. Mathew wrote in his ruling.
“Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false,” he said.
Jurors in September found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws for making misleading public statements about how it handled users’ personal data. The case was brought after political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica harvested Facebook data to generate targeted political ads during the 2016 election season.
The award will serve as a warning to tech companies that New Mexico will hold them accountable, state Attorney General Raúl Torrez said at a news conference.
“This judgment should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley,” he said.
Meta said the ruling and Torrez’s office’s approach to enforcement “makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico.”
“At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal,” C.J. Mahoney, the company’s chief legal officer, said in a statement.
The Menlo Park, California, company has a market value of $1.8 trillion and brought in more than $200 billion in revenue last year. Company shares traded 2% higher after Wednesday’s announcement, and it was scheduled to report its quarterly earnings later in the day.
New Mexico goes it alone
In August, Meta reached a settlement with nearly all states and territories — except New Mexico and Florida — to pay $18 billion and add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms.
The settlement ended a trial over teen social media addiction and resolved a pivotal case years in the making that sought to hold the tech giant accountable for the role its platforms played in undermining children’s mental health. The effort targeted features designed to grab young people’s attention.
New Mexico didn’t join the multistate settlement, choosing to go after the company on its own.
The director of a nonprofit that supports stronger policies toward corporations said $25 billion is “a drop in the bucket for Meta,” but demonstrates people want accountability.
“Right now, they are rolling out Muse, an AI assistant encouraging people to trust it with everything from their bank accounts to their medical information,” added Nidhi Hegde, executive director of the American Economic Liberties Project. “Which is why we need more enforcers with courage and laws with actual teeth to rein them in.”
At the trial, attorneys for the state cited a 2010 Washington Post op-ed in which Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote that the company didn’t sell user data.
“You have control over how your information is shared,” Zuckerberg said. “We do not and never will sell any of your information to anyone.”
New Mexico officials sought fines of $35 billion to $40 billion, arguing the company would only change if its stock price were impacted.

Facebook owner ordered to pay $25 billion after 87 million users caught up in data scandal
By Harry Dennis • Published: 22 Oct 2026 • 13:29 • 4 minutes read
Meta has been ordered to pay $25 billion over Facebook privacy claims. Credit: favoritesphoto / Shutterstock
Millions of Facebook users never took the quiz or or agreed to share their data, yet their details still ended up in the hands of Cambridge Analytica. A US judge has now ruled that Meta’s promise of user control was false, and the bill is bigger than anything the company has faced before.
A judge has ruled Facebook’s promise of control was false
A New Mexico judge has ordered Meta, the owner of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, to pay $25 billion (about €22.3 billion) after a jury found the company misled the public about how much control people had over their personal data. Judge Francis Mathew handed down the order on Wednesday October 21, writing that “Facebook promised users that the users controlled their data. This was false.” He added that the wrongdoing “goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices.”
It’s the largest penalty Meta has ever faced, and well above the $5 billion (€4.45 billion) the US Federal Trade Commission imposed over the same scandal in 2019. New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez called it one of the largest state verdicts against a company in American history, and said every dollar will go to the state’s schools.
Zuckerberg’s own messages were used against Meta
The case goes back to Cambridge Analytica, the British political consultancy that worked on Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign. It obtained the details of as many as 87 million Facebook users through a personality quiz app, with most of those people never having used the app themselves.
New Mexico sued in 2021, and on Friday September 25 jurors decided that 26 of 29 statements by Meta and its leadership were misleading, including how the company handled the fallout from the scandal. They then counted nearly 43.9 million violations of the state’s Unfair Practices Act, working the figure out from the number of people each statement reached.
The state argued that Meta lied to New Mexico users about who could access their data, and knew outside developers had broad access to it. Facebook’s own breakdown suggested the information of 348,472 people in the state may have been improperly shared.
Internal messages from Mark Zuckerberg were reportedly central to the judge’s findings. In one, he wrote that people “probably don’t understand their current privacy settings or care about who sees their updates.”
How $219 billion dropped to $25 billion
State law allows up to $5,000 (about €4,450) per violation, and the judge ruled that the full count supported a penalty of more than $219 billion (about €195 billion). He then cut it to $25 billion.
New Mexico had asked for between $35 billion and $40 billion (€31 billion to €35.6 billion), while Meta urged a cap of $3.45 billion (€3.07 billion), arguing anything larger would breach its right to due process.
Interest of 15 per cent a year will also build up while the appeal runs, according to the Associated Press. Torrez admitted the money will be tied up for now, though he still joked that the state “may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years.”
Spain was caught up in the original scandal too
Facebook’s own estimates in 2018 suggested the data of about 2.7 million people in the EU may have been exposed, with an estimated 137,000 of them in Spain. Only 44 people in Spain installed the quiz app themselves, yet the numbers climbed so high because it also reached into their friends’ accounts.
The New Mexico ruling doesn’t apply here, as it only covers that one US state. However, Spain has been taking its own action against Meta. In November 2025, a Madrid commercial court ordered the company to pay €479 million to 87 Spanish digital media outlets for breaking EU data protection rules (GDPR) in the way it used personal data for advertising, and Meta said it would appeal.
That same month, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced an investigation into claims that Meta used a hidden mechanism to track the web browsing of Android users and link it to their Facebook and Instagram accounts.
Meta will appeal, and the bill could shrink
Meta’s chief legal officer, C.J. Mahoney, said the ruling makes it “all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico” and described the case as an attempt to “impose a tax on speech.” He said the company is confident it will win on appeal, and its lawyers have called a penalty of this size “shocking to the conscience.”
Investors don’t seem too worried. Meta’s shares were trading about 2 per cent higher after the news, and analyst Gil Luria said the company “is worth nearly two trillion dollars and will likely continue to appeal.”
It isn’t Meta’s first loss in the state. Earlier this year, New Mexico won $942 million (€838 million) from the company in two trials over claims it misled young users about safety on Facebook and Instagram, and Meta settled with most other states in August, although New Mexico and Florida stayed out.
An appeal could also trim the total, since cutting the number of violations would cut the bill. Meanwhile, the judge has put off deciding on the state’s request for a court order forcing Meta to change how it handles user data until both sides have been heard again, so whether anything changes for ordinary Facebook users depends on that decision and on an appeal that experts expect to take years.

Meta ordered to pay $25 billion for deceiving users on privacy
Published 12:10 am Thursday, October 22, 2026
SAN FRANCISCO — A New Mexico judge on Wednesday ordered Meta to pay $25 billion for deceiving users about its data privacy practices, one of the largest penalties levied against a tech giant.
New Mexico sued Meta in 2021 over a scandal involving political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica, saying the social media company had misled users with its public statements about their data privacy. Last month, after a two-week trial, a jury in state District Court in Santa Fe ruled against Meta, saying the company had committed 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws. Each violation carried a penalty of up to $5,000.
On Wednesday, Judge Francis J. Mathew of state District Court in Santa Fe issued the landmark penalty, writing that the company and its executives purposefully misled the public.
“The harm in this matter is difficult to overstate, and goes to the heart of Facebook’s basic business proposition,” Mathew wrote in a 20-page judgment. He said the “extraordinary number of willful violations” that repeated over years “support the highest level of penalty.”
The order is the biggest blow yet to Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, as it has racked up court losses over the harms that its social media platforms have caused users. States and consumers have filed thousands of lawsuits over issues such as how Facebook and Instagram endangered child safety, led to social media addiction, used people’s data without their consent and infringed on their privacy.
New Mexico has been leading the charge against Meta, and winning. In August, a New Mexico judge ordered the company to pay $567 million in damages after a jury ruled the company had enabled harm to young users, on top of a $375 million penalty from the same case in March.
In both cases, New Mexico accused Meta of violating state consumer protection laws, which have emerged as an effective way to litigate tech companies that have been previously shielded by laws that protect free speech, said Vincent Joralemon, director of the Life Sciences Law and Policy Center at the Berkeley Center for Law and Technology.
“The takeaway from this will be that consumer protection laws will be the way to hold tech companies accountable,” Joralemon said, adding that the penalty could inspire other states to pursue similar lawsuits.
In August, Meta reached a landmark settlement with 47 states, the District of Columbia and U.S. territories, agreeing to pay up to $17.1 billion in penalties and make major changes to its products over claims that it endangered children with addictive social media platforms. As part of that settlement, Meta agreed to pay $459 million to settle similar privacy claims regarding Cambridge Analytica, meaning other states are unlikely to pursue the charges that New Mexico did.
New Mexico will apply the $25 billion awarded Wednesday toward a public education fund, according to the state.
“For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law,” Raúl Torrez, the attorney general of New Mexico, said in a statement. “Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable.”
Meta said it would appeal the decision.
“At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online,” C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said in a statement. “We are confident we will prevail on appeal.”
Some legal experts said the penalty could be the largest for any corporation from a jury verdict.
“It is a shockingly big number that jumps off the page,” said Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a think tank in Washington. “In the absence of congressional action, juries are stepping up to the plate.”
The data privacy case in New Mexico was in some ways a throwback to an earlier tech era, when social media — and not artificial intelligence — was in the spotlight. In 2018, The New York Times and other publications reported that British firm Cambridge Analytica had acquired the private data of tens of millions of Facebook users without their knowledge to build profiles of American voters.
The revelations set off an outcry over how Facebook was harvesting people’s information and treating their privacy. Facebook, like many social media platforms, is offered as a free digital service, but users provide their information to the sites and are targeted with ads. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg appeared in Congress to testify on his company’s handling of data.
During a two-week trial last month, lawyers for New Mexico presented evidence on how Meta’s executives mislead users with statements about their privacy. The lawyers contrasted public comments from Zuckerberg and Sheryl Sandberg, then Meta’s chief operating officer, against their private email conversations.
Meta’s lawyers argued that its users have the power to choose what data they share on the platform, and said its policies around third-party companies harvesting Facebook data had changed significantly since 2018.
Zuckerberg did not testify at the trial, but a video of his hour and half long deposition was shown to the jury.
The jurors ultimately found that 26 of the 29 statements made by Meta and its executives were unfair or deceptive.
New Mexico had asked for as much as $40 billion. Mathew awarded the state $219 billion in damages before reducing the penalty to $25 billion.
“Facebook was aware that its users did not understand its privacy settings and took advantage of that to a grossly unfair degree,” Mathew wrote, citing an email from Zuckerberg. “Facebook’s misrepresentations about users’ control of their data were not isolated incidents, but rather a systematic pattern of deception at the core of Facebook’s business model.”

Washington: A judge on Wednesday, October 21, ordered Meta to pay New Mexico USD 25 billion after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant.
Facebook’s conduct was intentional and executives consistently misled users about how the platform worked, state District Court Judge Francis J. Mathew wrote in his ruling.

State Attorney General Raúl Torrez said at a news conference that the award should be seen as a warning to tech companies that New Mexico will hold them accountable.
“This judgment should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley,” he said.
Representatives for Meta, which previously said it plans to appeal the September verdict, didn’t immediately respond to a message seeking comment about the amount. The Menlo Park, California-based company was scheduled to report its quarterly earnings Wednesday afternoon and its shares were trading 2 per cent higher following the penalty announcement.
New Mexico goes it alone
In August, Meta reached a settlement with nearly all states and territories — except New Mexico and Florida — to pay USD 18 billion and add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms.
The settlement ended a trial over teen social media addiction and resolved a pivotal case years in the making that sought to hold the tech giant accountable for the role its platforms played in undermining children’s mental health. The effort targeted features designed to grab young people’s attention.
New Mexico wasn’t part of the multistate settlement because it was pursuing its own case.
Jurors in September found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws when a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, harvested Facebook user data to generate targeted political ads for the 2016 election.
Attorneys for New Mexico had sought USD 35 billion to USD 40 billion, arguing that the company would only change its ways with a sum that affected its stock price.
Lawyers for Meta argued for paying no more than USD 3.4 billion. An award 10 times that or even more would violate due process, was unconstitutional and would not hold up under appeal, they said.
Meta argued the state failed to prove misleading statements about privacy and that content moderation actually harmed New Mexicans. Interest on the penalty would accrue during an appeal, but the number of violations Meta is charged with could be reduced.
Meta attorney Matt Nicholson argued in court that a sum as high as USD 40 billion would be “shocking to the conscience” while an attorney for New Mexico, Randi McGinn, urged standing up to “tech titans who think they are bulletproof and can do whatever they want.”
The amount awarded in the case far exceeds the USD 5 billion fine that the Federal Trade Commission levied against Facebook in 2019.
Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violations of consumer protection laws go toward state education spending. Torrez acknowledged the money would be tied up as Meta appeals.
Company argues that the state failed to prove harm
The state’s case focused on accusations that Facebook deceived users about a data breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, to generate targeted ads. The now-defunct firm’s clients included the 2016 campaign for President Donald Trump.
Attorneys for New Mexico argued that the state’s entire population, not just Facebook users, were deceived by the company’s public statements about privacy on the platform. Facebook’s lawyers argued that the state failed to prove whether people were actually harmed by these deceiving statements.
“The jury didn’t make findings that any New Mexican heard or saw these statements, or was harmed by them,” said Nicholson during a hearing Oct. 1.
New Mexico prosecutors also argued that Facebook allowed misinformation or violent content to proliferate on the platform. Defense attorneys vehemently denied the allegations, saying the company’s content moderation policies are robust and freedom of speech has to be considered.
Jury finds millions of violations
New Mexico was the only state to pursue a trial around the Cambridge Analytica scandal after 48 other states signed a settlement for USD 18 billion in August.
Besides New Mexico, Florida was the only other state that did not sign the settlement, which included an agreement to release Meta from future liability related to the Cambridge Analytica privacy breach.
During the trial, jurors assessed whether Facebook misled users about privacy and content moderation 34 separate times. State prosecutors, though, argued Facebook’s statements deceived the entire population of New Mexico and extended beyond social media users.
In the end, jurors agreed with this premise and found Facebook liable for 2.1 million violations on certain counts, bringing the total number of violations to over 43 million.
Facebook’s attorneys have argued in subsequent court filings that the state’s consumer protection laws don’t apply to people in New Mexico who weren’t using the platform at the time.
Torrez told reporters following the verdict that all money awarded will go into a fund for the state’s education system. The state is also seeking an injunction to stop similar practices.
Meta questions evidence and tally of violations
In appealing the jury’s verdict, Meta might reduce the number of violations and therefore the total financial penalty. Lawyers for the company said it was unprecedented for the state to count the number of violations based on how many individuals may have heard or seen the misleading statements from the company, arguing there was no evidence these statements ever harmed anyone.
During closing arguments, lawyers for Facebook said the state’s evidence was outdated and that despite having five years to gather material, New Mexico found only one other instance of a data breach.
In one of the few wins for the defense, jurors found the state didn’t prove that Facebook made false claims about removing harmful content, including misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic.
The state said the company favored certain accounts and allowed for violent or inaccurate content to proliferate. Attorney Randi McGinn said in her closing argument for the state that Facebook profited off harmful content, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg denied during his video deposition. Zuckerberg said the company has to carefully balance freedom of speech with content moderation.
Attorneys for Facebook said the company has adapted its policies since the state’s lawsuit was filed in 2021 and that it removes 99% of content that violates standards.

$25 billion. That's what a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay Wednesday over Facebook's privacy promises, after a September jury found more than 43 million violations of the state's consumer protection law. The state asked for as much as $40 billion. Apparently, this was the smaller bill.
State District Court Judge Francis J. Mathew laid out the problem in language that requires very little translation:
Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false. Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices.
New Mexico filed suit in 2021. Behind it was the personality quiz that collected Facebook information reaching far beyond the people who took it. Data from up to 87 million profiles was harvested, with Cambridge Analytica obtaining information for political targeting. The firm’s clients included Trump’s 2016 campaign.
Facebook said it would investigate. Mathew found that the promised comprehensive investigation never happened. Senior executives pushed to keep costs down, resources were inadequate, and the investigative methods fell short. The judge called the inquiry “willfully ineffective.” The investigation Facebook promised became evidence against it.
There's a consumer protection argument there, and it's not a weak one. Tell people they control their information, then let third parties access it without their knowledge, and you've got a problem. Whether a $25 billion problem is another question, and the one Meta's lawyers will be pressing on appeal.
The penalty takes a little more explaining.
The violation count came from multiplying misleading statements by their potential audiences. Mathew concluded that state law supported penalties exceeding $219 billion, then reduced the amount to $25 billion. New Mexico wanted $35 billion to $40 billion. Meta argued for a maximum of roughly $3.45 billion.
One of the state’s lawyers, Randi McGinn, explained its approach at an October 1 hearing:
"This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the value of its stock price. For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law."
That invites a fair question: How much of this penalty reflects the violations, and how much reflects officials’ determination to produce a number investors will notice?
The multiplication will sound familiar to readers of our earlier coverage of Meta’s child addiction litigation. That separate case carried a demand for $1.4 trillion. Statutory penalties add up quickly when the audience runs into the millions.
Meta's chief legal officer, C.J. Mahoney, calls the New Mexico lawsuit "a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico."
It's not a frivolous argument. Courts have pushed back on government attempts to police online content dressed up as consumer protection. Meta also argues the state never proved any consumer was actually harmed. Those arguments now have to clear a jury verdict and Mathew's findings, which won't be easy. But they're worth watching on appeal.

Meta ordered to pay billions in New Mexico Cambridge Analytica case
Santa Fe, New Mexico - Meta has been ordered to pay $25 billion in connection with the years-old Cambridge Analytica data privacy scandal, a judge in New Mexico announced on Wednesday.
A jury had previously found that Facebook misled users over privacy and free speech on the platform. The judge calculated the penalty at almost $219.5 billion, before reducing it to $25 billion in the same sentence.
In an initial response, Meta expressed confidence that it would win on appeal. After the jury's verdict a few weeks ago, the company said it disagreed with the decision and would continue to defend itself against the allegations.
Penalties of up to $5,000 had been set for each violation, and the jury found millions of violations, which added up to billions of dollars according to the judge's calculations.
The Cambridge Analytica scandal badly damaged public trust in Facebook in 2018. Information collected through what appeared to be an innocuous survey conducted by a data researcher was used to build user profiles and shared with political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica.
The team of Donald Trump, then a presidential candidate, also used the data before the 2016 presidential election. In total, around 87 million user accounts were affected.
Meta subsequently paid about $6 billion to the US government, among other measures, to settle investigations related to the case.
In the aftermath of the scandal, New Mexico took the company to court in 2021 with allegations concerning freedom of expression on the platform, prompted by revelations that emerged during the broader investigation into Facebook's practices.
Among other claims, a whistleblower report said that some prominent accounts had been secretly exempted from rules on content allowed on the platform.

sources.news_title: Meta Ordered To Pay New Mexico $25,000,000,000 After Jury Finds 43,899,720 Privacy Violations
sources.text:
Meta has been hit with the largest penalty in its history after a jury found the company misled users about how their data was protected.
New Mexico District Court Judge Francis J. Matthew ordered Meta on October 21st to pay $25 billion in civil penalties under the state’s Unfair Practices Act, says the New Mexico Department of Justice.
The order follows a September jury verdict finding that Facebook violated the law 43,899,725 times in connection with the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
In that scandal, a third-party personality quiz harvested data from roughly 87 million Facebook profiles that went to political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica to generate targeted ads for the election in 2016.
Judge Matthew set the penalty at the state’s maximum of $5,000 per violation, then reduced the resulting total of more than $219 billion to $25 billion, according to the judgment.
He also ordered interest to accrue at 15% a year until the penalty is paid in full.
Says Matthew,
“Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false.”
Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for consumer protection violations go toward state education spending.
Says Attorney General Raúl Torrez,
“This is a historic day for New Mexico and for consumers across the country. For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law. A New Mexico jury found nearly 44 million violations of our consumer protection statute, and this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences.”
Meta previously said it plans to appeal the September verdict and did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the amount, reports PBS NewsHour.
Meta argued that the state failed to demonstrate that the company made misleading claims about privacy or that its content moderation practices harmed New Mexico residents. The tech giant pushed for a penalty of no more than $3.4 billion.
New Mexico and Florida were the only states that did not join an $18 billion settlement Meta reached with nearly all states and territories in August, according to PBS.
The court put off a decision on the state’s request for an injunction pending further briefing.

sources.news_title: Meta ordered to pay $25-billion penalty to New Mexico in data privacy case
sources.text:
AT A GLANCE
- A New Mexico judge ordered Meta Platforms to pay $25 billion after a jury found the company misled consumers about data privacy, stemming from the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
- The ruling was described as one of the largest financial penalties against a corporation in US history, with New Mexico's Attorney General emphasizing the need to hold Big Tech accountable.
- Meta plans to appeal the decision, arguing that the penalties are excessive and that the state did not prove consumers were misled.
A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms on Wednesday, October 21, to pay the state $25 billion after a jury found the company had misled consumers about the privacy of their data, hitting the company with one of the largest financial penalties in US history.
The ruling came in a case stemming from allegations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign, obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their consent. New Mexico had sued Meta, accusing it of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data.
“Facebook’s wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order, which came more than three weeks after the verdict.
Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219 billion was warranted based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion.
In a statement, CJ Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal.
“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Mahoney said. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.”
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a statement after the ruling the penalty was one of the largest financial penalties against a corporation in US history.
Meta previously faced a $5-billion penalty from the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 over the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
Six other states settled their lawsuits against Meta related to Cambridge Analytica for $459.2 million as part of a $17.1 billion multistate settlement the company reached in August to resolve states’ claims that the company’s platforms had harmed teen mental health.
Lawsuit filed 5 years ago
New Mexico’s attorney general sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app.
The state accused Meta of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data and its handling of hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform. It alleged the company knew third parties had broad access to users’ data and tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company’s bottom line.
Cambridge Analytica, now defunct, used the data for voter profiling and targeting.
“It has been a long time coming holding Big Tech accountable,” Torrez told a press conference in Albuquerque after Wednesday’s ruling. “I think today’s judgment is a clear break with that past and a very clear warning to those in this space and beyond that we intend to protect our people and protect our consumers.”
Mathew’s decision comes as Meta faces thousands of lawsuits and pressure from lawmakers over the impact of Instagram and Facebook on teen mental health, with another trial slated to begin next week.
Earlier this year, New Mexico won $942 million in a pair oftrials against Meta over claims it facilitated sexual exploitation of young people on Instagram and Facebook and misled consumers about the platforms’ safety.
Analyst Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson & Co, called the latest New Mexico ruling costly but unlikely to impact the company’s value.
“Meta is worth nearly two trillion dollars, and will likely continue to appeal these cases and drag them out,” Luria said.
Experts expect long legal fight
Jurors in September had found that the company and its leadership made 26 misleading statements on data privacy, hate speech and other subjects. Multiplying those statements by their potential audience, they said the company had committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws.
At a hearing on October 1, Randi McGinn, a lawyer for New Mexico, had asked Mathew to award the state between $35 billion and $40 billion.
“This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the value of its stock price,” McGinn said.
In court filings, Meta urged Mathew to cap the penalties at $3.45 billion. The evidence showed that Meta does not sell user data and New Mexico did not prove that any consumer had actually been misled, the company said in court filings. – Rappler.com

sources.news_title: Meta Ordered To Pay Record $25 Billion in Cambridge Analytica-Linked Case After Judge Cuts $219 Billion Figure
sources.text:
Meta Ordered To Pay Record $25 Billion in Cambridge Analytica-Linked Case After Judge Cuts $219 Billion Figure
New Mexico refused an $18 billion deal and out-earned a 48-state coalition by trying Meta alone
Meta must pay New Mexico $25 billion (£19 billion) after a judge on Wednesday finalised one of the largest privacy-related penalties in Facebook's history, following a trial after New Mexico declined to join a multi-state settlement over separate child-safety claims.
A Record Penalty Years in the Making
Judge Francis Mathew entered the judgement on 21 October, ruling that New Mexico was entitled to $219.5 billion (£167 billion) under state law before cutting the figure to $25 billion. A Santa Fe jury in September found Meta committed nearly 43.9 million violations of New Mexico's Unfair Practices Act, each carrying a maximum $5,000 (£3,752) penalty.
The judgement is the latest courtroom setback for Meta in a bruising year. The award dwarfs the $5 billion (£3.752 billion) the Federal Trade Commission secured from Facebook over the same scandal in 2019, and it lands nearly a decade after Cambridge Analytica harvested data from more than 50 million users to target political adverts during the 2016 US election. Facebook knew of the misuse in December 2015 but did not tell the public until 2018, when a whistle-blower came forward.
One State's Gamble Pays Off
New Mexico's decision to pursue its case at trial contrasts with the multi-state settlement. In August, 47 states and several US territories reached an agreement with Meta worth up to $17.1 billion (£13 billion) over child-safety and social media addiction claims. New Mexico and Florida did not join the agreement, which addressed different claims from the Cambridge Analytica case.
The $25 billion judgement exceeds the announced value of that multi-state settlement, although the two cases involved different allegations. Attorney General Raúl Torrez, who called the result historic, had already won $942 million (£706.88 million) from Meta this year in a separate case over protections for children. Facebook's published breakdown said information from 348,472 New Mexico users may have been improperly shared in the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
The trial featured a video deposition of Zuckerberg, and at a hearing on 1 October state lawyer Randi McGinn asked for between $35 billion and $40 billion (£26.26 to 30 billion). Mathew landed well below the state's request, but far above every earlier privacy settlement the company has signed.
Zuckerberg's Own Words Sink Meta
Mathew leaned heavily on Mark Zuckerberg's internal messages. The judge found the chief executive knew users struggled to grasp Facebook's controls and exploited it, citing Zuckerberg's own line that people 'probably don't understand their current privacy settings or care about who sees their updates'.
In another message, Zuckerberg suggested the company give users 'a chance to change their privacy settings but obviously don't encourage it'. Mathew ruled that Facebook's controls failed to give users meaningful command of their data, and that outside developers could still reach it.
Meta Vows To Appeal
Meta will challenge the judgement. Chief Legal Officer C.J. Mahoney said the ruling 'makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico' and accused Torrez of conflating privacy with free speech. The lawsuit, he argued, 'seeks to impose a tax on speech' to police what people say online.
The appeal could run for years, and the sum may yet shrink again. Still, the verdict shows a lone state attorney general can force Big Tech to answer for privacy deception long after the headlines fade, with a judgement exceeding the announced value of a separate multi-state settlement.

sources.news_title: Meta ordered to pay US$25b over Facebook user deception in Cambridge Analytica case
sources.text:
SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 22 — A New Mexico judge ruled Wednesday that Meta must pay US$25 billion (RM102 billion) to the state after a jury found last month that the social media giant had deceived users in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal, according to media reports.
The penalty comes a couple of months after Meta agreed to pay US$18 billion to settle claims brought by 48 other states, including allegations tied to Cambridge Analytica.
Meta slammed the case as “a tax on speech.”
“This ruling... makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Meta said in a statement. “We are confident we will prevail on appeal.”
Cambridge Analytica was a political consulting firm found to have improperly harvested personal data from millions of Facebook users for targeted political advertising, notably during the 2016 US presidential election.
Revelations at the time showed that the firm had obtained data gathered through a personality quiz app called “thisisyourdigitallife,” which was installed by about 270,000 users but also collected information on their friends.
In total, the app reached roughly 87 million Facebook users worldwide.
Facebook learned in December 2015 that Cambridge Analytica had acquired the data but did not disclose it publicly until 2018, after a whistleblower came forward, sparking a major political scandal.
Jurors in the New Mexico trial found that the misconduct affected all of the state’s more than 2.1 million residents.
“We disagree with the verdict and will continue to defend ourselves against efforts to distort our record,” a Meta spokesperson said in a statement in September.
New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez hailed the ruling as a “historic” win.
This case was “about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences. New Mexico stood its ground,” Torrez said in a statement.
Penalties pile up
Meta has faced a slew of lawsuits in recent months.
Earlier this year, New Mexico won nearly US$1 billion in combined penalties against Meta in a separate case over harms to children.
In March, a jury in that case ordered Meta to pay US$375 million after finding the company liable for endangering children by making them vulnerable to predators on its platforms, among other harms.
In August, a judge ordered Meta to implement product changes and pay an additional US$567 million to the state to fund the treatment and prevention of harms caused by Facebook and Instagram.
That same month, Meta agreed to pay up to US$17.7 billion to 52 US states, plus Washington, DC, to settle claims that it deliberately engineered its platforms to hook young users, misled the public about the risks and unlawfully collected data from children under 13.
As part of that settlement, Meta agreed to make significant changes to Facebook and Instagram accounts used by teenagers, and portions of the settlement hinge on other major social media companies agreeing to similar changes.
In September, TikTok agreed to pay Alabama at least US$100 million and enact limits for teen users, avoiding a trial over claims related to child safety on the platform.
TikTok previously settled other cases that were headed for trial, including a Los Angeles lawsuit brought by a young woman and a suit from a Kentucky school district.
In a landmark trial that concluded in March, Meta and YouTube were convicted by a Los Angeles jury, which found both companies were responsible for a teenager’s social media addiction.
That jury awarded the teenager US$6 million. — AFP

sources.news_title: Meta $25 Billion Fine in New Mexico Privacy Case
sources.text:
Meta Platforms has been ordered to pay $25 billion in civil penalties after a New Mexico judge ruled that the company violated state consumer protection laws by misleading the public about Facebook user data and its content moderation practices.
The ruling, reported by the BBC on October 22, follows a jury verdict that found Facebook committed nearly 43.9 million violations of New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act. The case examined the company’s statements about how it collected, protected, shared and used personal information, as well as its claims about addressing misinformation and hate speech.
Judge Francis Mathew issued the penalty after the jury found the company liable in September. The court calculated the potential penalty at approximately $219.5 billion but reduced it to $25 billion, according to the report.
The lawsuit, brought by New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez, stemmed in part from the Cambridge Analytica scandal, which drew international attention to the use of Facebook users’ personal information by third parties. The British political consulting firm obtained data from millions of Facebook users, raising concerns about how personal information could be accessed and used for political purposes, including during the 2016 US presidential election.
New Mexico’s case extended beyond data privacy. State lawyers also accused Meta of misleading the public about its handling of harmful content and the enforcement of platform rules. The jury found the company had violated state law through misleading statements on these issues.
Meta disputed the allegations and said it intended to appeal the ruling. The company argued that the lawsuit sought to restrict online speech and impose new rules on what users could say on its platforms.
The ruling adds to the legal pressure facing Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. In 2019, the company agreed to pay a $5 billion penalty to the US Federal Trade Commission over privacy violations following a separate investigation into its data practices.
The New Mexico decision comes as Meta increases investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure. The company has said it expects to spend heavily on AI development, even as it faces scrutiny over the safety and effects of its social media platforms.
The court’s order sets the civil penalty at $25 billion, although Meta’s planned appeal means the ruling remains subject to further legal proceedings.

sources.news_title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion to New Mexico in Cambridge Analytica case
sources.text:
A New Mexico judge ruled Wednesday that Meta must pay $25 billion to the state after a jury found last month that the social media giant had deceived users in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal, according to media reports.
The penalty comes a couple of months after Meta agreed to pay $18 billion to settle claims brought by 48 other states, including allegations tied to Cambridge Analytica.
Meta slammed the case as "a tax on speech."
"This ruling... makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Meta said in a statement. "We are confident we will prevail on appeal."
Cambridge Analytica was a political consulting firm found to have improperly harvested personal data from millions of Facebook users for targeted political advertising, notably during the 2016 US presidential election.
Revelations at the time showed that the firm had obtained data gathered through a personality quiz app called "thisisyourdigitallife," which was installed by about 270,000 users but also collected information on their friends.
In total, the app reached roughly 87 million Facebook users worldwide.
Facebook learned in December 2015 that Cambridge Analytica had acquired the data but did not disclose it publicly until 2018, after a whistleblower came forward, sparking a major political scandal.
Jurors in the New Mexico trial found that the misconduct affected all of the state's more than 2.1 million residents.
"We disagree with the verdict and will continue to defend ourselves against efforts to distort our record," a Meta spokesperson said in a statement in September.
New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez hailed the ruling as a "historic" win.
This case was "about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences. New Mexico stood its ground," Torrez said in a statement.
Meta has faced a slew of lawsuits in recent months.
Earlier this year, New Mexico won nearly $1 billion in combined penalties against Meta in a separate case over harms to children.
In March, a jury in that case ordered Meta to pay $375 million after finding the company liable for endangering children by making them vulnerable to predators on its platforms, among other harms.
In August, a judge ordered Meta to implement product changes and pay an additional $567 million to the state to fund the treatment and prevention of harms caused by Facebook and Instagram.
That same month, Meta agreed to pay up to $17.7 billion to 52 US states, plus Washington, DC, to settle claims that it deliberately engineered its platforms to hook young users, misled the public about the risks and unlawfully collected data from children under 13.
As part of that settlement, Meta agreed to make significant changes to Facebook and Instagram accounts used by teenagers, and portions of the settlement hinge on other major social media companies agreeing to similar changes.
In September, TikTok agreed to pay Alabama at least $100 million and enact limits for teen users, avoiding a trial over claims related to child safety on the platform.
TikTok previously settled other cases that were headed for trial, including a Los Angeles lawsuit brought by a young woman and a suit from a Kentucky school district.
In a landmark trial that concluded in March, Meta and YouTube were convicted by a Los Angeles jury, which found both companies were responsible for a teenager's social media addiction.
That jury awarded the teenager $6 million.

In the Cambridge Analytica scandal, the now-defunct UK political consulting firm obtained personal information from as many as 87 million Facebook users and used the data for political profiling and targeted advertising. This is Meta’s second major courtroom loss in New Mexico this year.
In a separate case involving the safety of young users, a jury in March imposed $375 million in civil penalties on the company. On Aug. 6, a judge ordered Meta to pay an additional $567 million into a fund for youth mental-health remedies and imposed court-supervised changes to Facebook and Instagram, bringing the total financial exposure in that case to $942 million.

sources.news_title: Meta ordered to pay $25B to N.M.
sources.text:
A judge on Wednesday ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant.
Facebook's deception was intentional and executives consistently misled users about how the platform worked, state District Court Judge Francis J. Mathew wrote in his ruling.
"Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false," he said.
Jurors in September found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws for making misleading public statements about how it handled users' personal data. The case was brought after political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica harvested Facebook data to generate targeted political ads during the 2016 election season.
The award will serve as a warning to tech companies that New Mexico will hold them accountable, state Attorney General Raúl Torrez said at a news conference.
"This judgment should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley," he said.
Meta said the ruling and Torrez's office's approach to enforcement "makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico."
"At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal," C.J. Mahoney, the company's chief legal officer, said in a statement.
The Menlo Park, Calif., company has a market value of $1.8 trillion and brought in more than $200 billion in revenue last year. Company shares traded 2% higher after Wednesday's announcement, and ended the day's trading roughly 0.5% higher.
In August, Meta reached a settlement with nearly all states and territories -- except New Mexico and Florida -- to pay $18 billion and add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms.
The settlement ended a trial over teen social media addiction and resolved a pivotal case years in the making that sought to hold the tech giant accountable for the role its platforms played in undermining children's mental health. The effort targeted features designed to grab young people's attention.
New Mexico didn't join the multistate settlement, choosing to go after the company on its own.
The director of a nonprofit that supports stronger policies toward corporations said $25 billion is "a drop in the bucket for Meta," but demonstrates people want accountability.
"Right now, they are rolling out Muse, an AI assistant encouraging people to trust it with everything from their bank accounts to their medical information," added Nidhi Hegde, executive director of the American Economic Liberties Project. "Which is why we need more enforcers with courage and laws with actual teeth to rein them in."
At the trial, attorneys for the state cited a 2010 Washington Post op-ed in which Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote that the company didn't sell user data.
"You have control over how your information is shared," Zuckerberg said. "We do not and never will sell any of your information to anyone."
New Mexico officials sought fines of $35 billion to $40 billion, arguing the company would only change if its stock price were impacted.
Meta's lawyers, meanwhile, asserted that the state failed to prove the company made misleading statements and that content moderation actually harmed people in New Mexico. They wanted the company to pay $3.4 billion at most and said an award many times larger would be unconstitutional.
Although interest would accrue on the penalty during the appeal process, Meta could succeed in reducing the number of violations for which it is found liable.
The $25 billion award far exceeds a $5 billion fine the Federal Trade Commission levied against Facebook in 2019.
Peter Ormerod, an associate law professor at Villanova University, was surprised by the size of the New Mexico judgment because previous legal settlements over Cambridge Analytica were much lower.
"It comes out to about $12,000 per person in New Mexico," he said. "It's quite unlike anything else we've seen."
Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violating consumer protection laws go toward education spending. It could take years for the state to get the money while the company appeals.
The trial focused on accusations Facebook deceived users about a breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to Cambridge Analytica. The now-defunct firm's clients included Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign.
Attorneys for New Mexico argued that the state's entire population was deceived, and that Facebook allowed misinformation or violent content to proliferate.
Meta's lawyers argued the state failed to prove people were harmed by deceptive statements. Zuckerberg in a video deposition denied that Facebook profited off harmful content and said the company had to balance free speech with content moderation.
In a partial win for the company, jurors rejected assertions that Facebook made false claims about removing harmful content, including misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic.
Meta lawyers said it has changed policies since the lawsuit was filed in 2021 and catches and removes an estimated 99% of content violating its standards.
Information for this article was contributed by Matthew Brown and Barbara Ortutay of The Associated Press.

“This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."

Cambridge Analytica, now defunct, used the data for voter profiling and targeting.
"It has been a long time coming holding Big Tech accountable," Torrez told a press conference in Albuquerque after Wednesday's ruling. "I think today's judgment is a clear break with that past and a very clear warning to those in this space and beyond that we intend to protect our people and protect our consumers."

In August, Meta reached a settlement with nearly all states and territories — except New Mexico and Florida — to pay $US18 billion ($25.6 billion) and add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms.
The settlement ended a trial over teenage social media addiction and resolved a pivotal case years in the making that sought to hold the tech giant accountable for the role its platforms played in undermining children's mental health.

During the trial, prosecutors cited a 2010 Washington Post op-ed from Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg, in which he wrote that the company did not sell user data.
