sources.text:
By Kevin Hendricks, NM Political Report — Meta now has a $25 billion reason to read the fine print.
District Judge Francis Mathew ordered Meta Platforms Inc. on Wednesday to pay New Mexico $25 billion for misleading Facebook users about their privacy, misinformation, hate speech and more. The bill grows 15% a year until Meta pays, roughly $10.3 million a day.
Mathew ruled that the jury’s 43,899,725 violations justified the law’s maximum $5,000 per violation, nearly $219.5 billion. He then cut the total to $25 billion, about $570 per violation.
“Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable,” Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a statement. His office called it one of the largest penalties against a corporation in U.S. history.
How the judge got there
Mathew pointed to 26 deceptive statements spanning more than 11 years, many from CEO Mark Zuckerberg and former COO Sheryl Sandberg. Facebook kept making those promises after its own employees warned it couldn’t keep them, he found.
After the Cambridge Analytica scandal, Facebook vowed to tell users when apps misused their data. It notified users of just two apps out of thousands, the order says. Apps tied to misuse touched data from at least 1.1 million New Mexicans.
The order also quotes a private Zuckerberg email about rolling out a privacy change: “Give them a chance to change their privacy settings but obviously don’t encourage it.”
Meta’s side
At a hearing this month, Meta asked the judge to limit the penalty to $3.45 billion, while the state asked for $35 billion to $40 billion. Meta attorney Matthew Nicholson argued a massive fine would violate the excessive-fines protections in both the state and U.S. constitutions, and that the state never showed any New Mexican saw, relied on or was harmed by the statements.
Torrez said Meta has signaled it will appeal.
What happens next
Mathew held off on injunctive relief, such as the independent monitor the state wants, pending more briefing. An appeal could take three or four years, Torrez said, and the 15% interest keeps running the whole time.
Once the money arrives, the state constitution dedicates Unfair Practices Act penalties to school construction and other capital projects, Torrez said. At $25 billion, he joked, the state “may have in fact paid for the construction of schools” for the next several hundred years.
New Mexico went it alone. Meta paid $459 million this summer to resolve cases from 46 states and two territories. Torrez said he’d let others decide whether $25 billion for one state counts as a victory.
It’s the state’s second big win over Meta this year. In a separate child safety case, a jury ordered $375 million in March and a judge added $567 million in August, bringing the state’s total against Meta to nearly $26 billion.
Torrez wants lawmakers to rewrite the Unfair Practices Act in the coming session. The $5,000 penalty cap hasn’t been adjusted for inflation in more than 50 years, he said.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg speaks with Co-Chair of the US President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology David Sacks, as President Donald Trump speaks to the press at the White House driveway following a luncheon for tech leaders in the East Room, in Washington, D.C., US, September 29, 2026. REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst
A judge unloaded on a company run by one of President Donald Trump's most powerful tech allies for years of deliberate deception.
New Mexico state court Judge Francis Mathew ordered Mark Zuckerberg's Meta Platforms to pay a $25 billion civil penalty for misleading the public about Facebook's privacy practices after the Cambridge Analytica scandal, Bloomberg Law reported Wednesday. The sum ranks among the largest ever handed down by an American court.
The judgment follows a Santa Fe jury's finding last month that Meta violated New Mexico's Unfair Practices Act more than 43 million times. Jurors concluded that the company and its leaders repeatedly misled the public about how Facebook protected user data and policed hate speech.
Mathew pointed to "the clearly intentional and systemic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements" in justifying the award, adding that the company's misconduct "goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices."
He went further elsewhere in the ruling, according to reporting by Courthouse News.
"Facebook's misrepresentations about users' control of their data were not isolated incidents, but rather a systemic pattern of deception at the core of Facebook's business model," Mathew wrote.
The state law allows up to $5,000 per violation. Mathew found the maximum was warranted, which would have pushed the total past $219 billion, but he trimmed it to $25 billion, below the $35 billion to $40 billion the state sought, according to Bloomberg Law. The penalty carries 15 percent annual interest until Meta pays in full.
The total outstrips the $14.8 billion in general-fund revenue New Mexico expects to collect in fiscal 2028.
The case stems from the scandal in which political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica harvested data from millions of Facebook users to target voters on Trump's behalf ahead of the 2016 election. Zuckerberg has since moved closer to Trump. He joined other tech executives at the White House for a meeting on artificial intelligence last month.
Meta Chief Legal Officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement that "we are confident we will prevail on appeal."

sources.news_title: Cambridge Analytica case: Judge orders Meta to pay $25bn to New Mexico
sources.text:
A New Mexico judge ruled Wednesday that Meta must pay $25 billion to the state after a jury found last month that the social media giant had deceived users in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal, according to media reports.
The penalty comes a couple of months after Meta agreed to pay $18 billion to settle claims brought by 48 other states, including allegations tied to Cambridge Analytica.
Meta slammed the case as “a tax on speech.”
“This ruling… makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Meta said in a statement. “We are confident we will prevail on appeal.”
Cambridge Analytica was a political consulting firm found to have improperly harvested personal data from millions of Facebook users for targeted political advertising, notably during the 2016 US presidential election.
Revelations at the time showed that the firm had obtained data gathered through a personality quiz app called “thisisyourdigitallife,” which was installed by about 270,000 users but also collected information on their friends.
In total, the app reached roughly 87 million Facebook users worldwide.
Facebook learned in December 2015 that Cambridge Analytica had acquired the data but did not disclose it publicly until 2018, after a whistleblower came forward, sparking a major political scandal.
Jurors in the New Mexico trial found that the misconduct affected all of the state’s more than 2.1 million residents.
“We disagree with the verdict and will continue to defend ourselves against efforts to distort our record,” a Meta spokesperson said in a statement in September.
New Mexico Attorney-General Raul Torrez hailed the ruling as a “historic” win.
This case was “about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences. New Mexico stood its ground,” Torrez said in a statement.
– Penalties pile up –
Meta has faced a slew of lawsuits in recent months.
Earlier this year, New Mexico won nearly $1 billion in combined penalties against Meta in a separate case over harms to children.
In March, a jury in that case ordered Meta to pay $375 million after finding the company liable for endangering children by making them vulnerable to predators on its platforms, among other harms.
In August, a judge ordered Meta to implement product changes and pay an additional $567 million to the state to fund the treatment and prevention of harms caused by Facebook and Instagram.
That same month, Meta agreed to pay up to $17.7 billion to 52 US states, plus Washington, DC, to settle claims that it deliberately engineered its platforms to hook young users, misled the public about the risks and unlawfully collected data from children under 13.
As part of that settlement, Meta agreed to make significant changes to Facebook and Instagram accounts used by teenagers, and portions of the settlement hinge on other major social media companies agreeing to similar changes.
In September, TikTok agreed to pay Alabama at least $100 million and enact limits for teen users, avoiding a trial over claims related to child safety on the platform.
TikTok previously settled other cases that were headed for trial, including a Los Angeles lawsuit brought by a young woman and a suit from a Kentucky school district.
In a landmark trial that concluded in March, Meta and YouTube were convicted by a Los Angeles jury, which found both companies were responsible for a teenager’s social media addiction.
That jury awarded the teenager $6 million.

sources.text:
BREAKING: Meta Forced to Pay $25 Billion Settlement for Privacy Breach
A state judge in New Mexico slapped Meta with one of the largest penalties on record for a tech company, ordering it to pay $25 billion for privacy violations and intentional misstatements.
The judgment came following a two-week trial in which a jury ruled against Meta, finding it liable for 43 million violations of state consumer protection laws in New Mexico, Mediaite reported.
Each violation will cost the big tech giant $5,000.
Judge Francis J. Mathew of the State District Court in Santa Fe lowered the initial amount of $200 billion, but ruled that Meta will face a 15 percent interest rate for each year that the sum goes unpaid.
Mathew wrote, “The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook’s repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act — $5,000 per violation found by the jury.”
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez commented on the decision, saying, “The jury’s verdict is a historic victory for every child and family who has paid the price for Meta’s choice to put profits over kids’ safety.”
“Meta executives knew their products harmed children, disregarded warnings from their own employees, and lied to the public about what they knew,” he added. “Today the jury joined families, educators, and child safety experts in saying enough is enough.”
New Mexico prosecutors argued that Facebook deceived consumers regarding a data breach from a third party, which was gathering information and selling it to Cambridge Analytica, a political consulting firm.
Torrez had previously accused Meta of failing to protect children on its platforms from child predators, abuse, and human trafficking.
“Our investigation into Meta’s social media platforms demonstrates that they are not safe spaces for children but rather prime locations for predators to trade child pornography and solicit minors for sex,” he said after filing the lawsuit back in 2023.
He said this recent ruling should deter other tech companies from making the same mistake, adding that the money will fund education in New Mexico.
“This judgement should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley,” the state attorney general concluded.
Meta plans to appeal, however, with Chief Legal Officer C.J. Mahoney saying that the company is confident the courts will rule in its favor, Reuters reported.
“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” he said. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.”

Meta hit with $25-billion penalty for misleading Facebook users about data privacy

Meta, the parent company of Facebook, was ordered by a New Mexico judge on Wednesday to pay $25 billion for misleading users about how it collects and safeguards user data.
The penalty, one of the largest ever levied against Meta or any other company, is the latest legal hit to the social media giant, which has grappled with lawsuits over allegations of social media addiction and child safety.
New Mexico sued the company in 2021 after revelations surfaced that a U.K. political consulting firm had harvested millions of Facebook users’ personal data without their consent. The major data privacy scandal sparked more scrutiny of Facebook and led to lawsuits, congressional hearings and multibillion-dollar fines.
A New Mexico jury dealt a blow to Meta, previously named Facebook, in September, finding that the social media company committed 43 million violations of the state’s consumer protection laws by making false and misleading statements about data privacy protections and efforts to combat misinformation and hate speech.
“Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable,” New Mexico state Atty. Gen. Raúl Torrez said in a statement.
As part of the jury’s ruling, Meta faced up to $5,000 for each willful violation, according to a news release about the verdict.
Meta said in a statement it plans to appeal the ruling.
“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico. At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal,” C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said in a statement.
Facebook was found to have deceived its users through statements and remarks made on its own platforms, interviews, earnings calls and other channels. The social media platform has privacy settings, but “they do not provide any meaningful control over their data in many ways,” and the company intentionally tried to mislead the public, according to the court’s judgment in the New Mexico case.
The judgment also found that Facebook committed to notifying users when an app misused their data and deliberately didn’t.
Meta made misleading statements about whether it sells people’s data and profits from misinformation or hate speech, along with other practices, the New Mexico jury found.
Meta has long grappled with data privacy lawsuits and complaints. The company has expanded beyond social networking and sells consumer gadgets, including smart glasses, that have also raised privacy concerns after allegations that people are being recorded without their knowledge.
The company has suffered from several high-profile legal blows this year that have resulted in multibillion-dollar penalties. In August, Meta agreed to pay $17 billion to resolve a child safety lawsuit filed by California and other states.
The company lost a child safety case in Los Angeles. New Mexico has also imposed other penalties on Meta this year. A New Mexico court ordered Meta to pay $942 million and take steps to make the platform safer after the state sued the company over allegations that it violated state consumer protection laws and enabled mental health harms to and sexual exploitation of young people.
In 2025, Meta reported roughly $200 billion in annual revenue and $60 billion in net income.
Meta reported third-quarter revenue of $64 billion on Wednesday, beating Wall Street’s expectations. But legal expenses totaling roughly $10 billion tied to the August agreement to resolve the case over the mental health of young people did affect Meta’s bottom line.
The company’s operating income that quarter was $13 billion, down 37% from the same period last year because of the legal costs.
Meta’s stock was up around 4% in after-hours trading.

sources.news_title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion in New Mexico case over Cambridge Analytica scandal
sources.text:
New York (CNN) — A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after the company was found to have misled users about its privacy practices in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
The Wednesday ruling marks one of the largest-ever legal penalties for a tech giant — and just the latest court loss for Meta this year.
The company, then known as Facebook, disclosed in 2018 that the private information of as many as 87 million Facebook users was improperly obtained by political analytics firm Cambridge Analytica. The firm used that information to build profiles of American voters.
New Mexico sued Facebook in 2021, accusing it of mishandling state residents’ personal information and deceiving those users about its policies in connection with the incident.
A jury found in September that Meta had violated the state’s Unfair Practices Act more than 43 million times. State District Court Judge Francis Mathew criticized the company for what he described as a “coherent strategy designed to mislead the public” in his Wednesday penalty decision.
“Facebook’s misrepresentations about users’ control of their data were not isolated incidents, but rather a systematic pattern of deception at the core of Facebook’s business model,” Mathew wrote.
After Wednesday’s penalty decision, Meta said it will appeal the decision and has accused New Mexico’s attorney general of conflating privacy and speech issues.
“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Meta Chief Legal Officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal.”
Meta’s legal battles threaten to strain its business, though court penalties and settlements remain relatively small compared to the company’s earnings so far.
The company reported earnings for the quarter ended in September on Wednesday, including lower quarterly profits than Wall Street had expected. It attributed the miss to a charge from the $18 billion multistate settlement it agreed to in August to resolve claims that its platforms have addicted and harmed young people.
New Mexico was not a party to that settlement, which also resolved the participating states’ outstanding claims related to Cambridge Analytica.
Meta posted income from operations of nearly $13 billion during the quarter, compared to nearly $23 billion that it said it would have earned without the settlement.
Meta CFO Susan Li said on a call with analysts following the earnings report that the company is monitoring “active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results,” including additional youth-related trials set for later this year and next.
Meta was also ordered to pay nearly $1 billion in a separate New Mexico case earlier this year over claims that its platforms addicted and harmed young people. Meta, along with YouTube, also lost a case in March in Los Angeles brought by a young woman with similar addiction and harm claims. The companies plan to appeal.
Meta earnings
Still, Meta’s business continues to grow at a strong clip thanks in large part to its investments in artificial intelligence. The company posted sales growth of 26% year-on-year to more than $64 billion in the quarter.
Meta’s stock (META) jumped more than 3% in after-hours trading following the report on Wednesday.
Meta launched its Muse AI personal assistant app in September. The app quickly rocketed to the top of app stores and has gained more than 10 million users, according to the company. It also launched its latest foundation model, Muse Wonder, last month.
The company said Wednesday that its AI investments are boosting its core advertising business “through stronger engagement, better recommendations, and more efficient monetization.” Its average price per ad, a key metric for the company, jumped 14% year-over-year in the September quarter.
Across the industry, tech companies face questions about their heavy spending on AI infrastructure. Meta’s capital expenditures during the quarter reached nearly $35 billion, up 80% from the year-ago quarter. And the company narrowed its full-year capital expenditure guidance to between $135 billion to $145 billion, the upper end of the range it had previously provided. Meta declined to provide spending guidance for next year.
But investors are signaling they’re willing to give Meta some leeway, given the success of Muse, said Jesse Cohen, senior analyst at Investing.com.
“The market has shifted from punishing Meta for spending to rewarding it for having a compelling product story,” Cohen wrote in emailed commentary.

The case stems from the Cambridge Analytica scandal, over which New Mexico sued in 2021. The New York Times reported that the order from Judge Francis J. Mathew of the State District Court in Santa Fe "is the biggest blow yet to Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, as it has racked up court losses over the harms that its social media platforms have caused users."
Reuters noted that "in 2019, the company was hit with a $5 billion penalty by the US Federal Trade Commission stemming from the same scandal. However, Torrez's state wasn't part of that settlement—and last month, a jury found that Meta had committed over 43 million violations of the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act.
That led to the order in which Mathew wrote that "the extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act—$5,000 per violation found by the jury."
Although the judge ultimately reduced the penalty to just over 11% of what Meta could have faced, the tech giant is still trying to dodge it. Chief legal officer CJ Mahoney said in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal."
"This ruling, and the attorney general’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."
Meanwhile, Torrez celebrated "a historic day for New Mexico and for consumers across the country."
"For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," the attorney general said. "A New Mexico jury found nearly 44 million violations of our consumer protection statute, and this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences. We took on one of the largest companies in the world because New Mexicans deserve honesty, accountability, and the protection of their personal information. Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable."
"This case has always been about more than one company or one scandal,” Torrez stressed. "It is about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences. New Mexico stood its ground, took this case to trial, and secured a verdict establishing millions of violations of our law. This outcome reinforces a fundamental principle, companies that do business in our state must follow our laws and respect the rights of our people."
It isn't Torrez's first victory against Meta. In August, Judge Bryan Biedscheid of the State District Court in Santa Fe tacked on $567 million in damages for a state case in which the company already faced $375 million in civil penalties for enabling harm to youth.

sources.text:
Meta ordered to pay $25B after jury finds it misled users on data privacy
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said the ruling was one of the largest ever against Meta by a single state
Meta Platforms has been ordered to pay $25 billion after a New Mexico jury found the company misled Facebook users over its handling of personal data and other practices in a case stemming from the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
New Mexico Judge Francis Mathew issued the penalty Wednesday after jurors found last month that Meta made dozens of misleading statements to users.
"Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices," Mathew wrote in his order.
The now-defunct Cambridge Analytica, which worked for President Donald Trump's 2016 campaign, obtained information from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app without their consent.
META PUTS POPULAR NEW TOOL IN HANDS OF SMALL BUSINESSES
New Mexico sued Meta in 2021, accusing the company of misleading users about who could access their personal information and how it handled harmful content on the platform.
Jurors found that 26 of 29 statements examined during the trial were misleading and determined that Meta committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico's consumer protection laws.
Mathew said the violations could have resulted in a penalty of more than $219 billion under state law but ultimately reduced the amount to $25 billion. Meta had urged Mathew to limit the penalty to $3.45 billion.
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said the ruling was one of the largest ever against Meta by a single state.
"It has been a long time coming holding Big Tech accountable," Torrez said.
"I think today's judgment is a clear break with that past and a very clear warning to those in this space and beyond that we intend to protect our people and protect our consumers."
META SETTLES FEDERAL TRIAL OVER CLAIMS FACEBOOK, INSTAGRAM ADDICT CHILDREN
Meta said it plans to appeal the ruling.
"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," C.J. Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said in a statement.
"At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal. In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge."

sources.news_title: Judge orders Meta to pay $25bn in fines for Facebook privacy violations
sources.text:
Judge orders Meta to pay $25bn in fines for Facebook privacy violations
A jury found Meta guilty of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about access to their data.
A United States judge has ordered Meta to pay $25bn after a jury found the company misled Facebook users about privacy violations, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant.
New Mexico state District Judge Francis Mathew issued the ruling on Wednesday.
“Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false,” he said.
Last month, a jury found Meta responsible for more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws. New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez highlighted that the decision was one of the largest state verdicts against a company in US history.
“This judgement should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley,” Torrez said at a news conference.
Meta lawyer Matt Nicholson argued in court that a sum as high as $40bn would be “shocking to the conscience”, while a lawyer for New Mexico, Randi McGinn, urged standing up to “tech titans who think they are bulletproof and can do whatever they want”.
“The jury didn’t make findings that any New Mexican heard or saw these statements, or was harmed by them,” Nicholson argued during a hearing held early this month.
Torrez told reporters following the verdict that all the money awarded would go into a fund for the state’s education system.
The amount awarded in the case far exceeds the $5bn fine that the Federal Trade Commission levied against Facebook in 2019.
New Mexico accused Meta of misleading users about who could access their personal information and how harmful content was handled on its platforms. Jurors found that 26 of 29 statements made by Meta and its leadership on privacy and content moderation were misleading.
Meta plans to appeal the verdict, potentially reducing the final payment amount.
In a statement, CJ Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal.
“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Mahoney said. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.”
The lawsuit, filed in 2021, stemmed partly from revelations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm that is now defunct, had obtained personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users without their consent and used it to develop targeted political advertisements. Its clients included President Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign.
The case, a major setback for the tech giant, marks the second legal defeat for Meta in New Mexico in six months. In March, a jury found the company misled users about the safety of young people on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, ordering it to pay $375m in civil penalties. Meta was later ordered to make an additional $567m payment into a state fund for teen mental health and was required to implement measures to protect young users.

sources.news_title: Judge Orders Meta to Pay $25 Billion in Data Privacy Case
sources.text:
A New Mexico judge has ruled that Meta owes $25 billion in penlties after being found liable of allowing a third party to harvest user data and misleading users about how their data was taken and what it was being used for.
The judgement follows the Cambridge Analytica case from the 2010s, in which a firm gathered Facebook user data by having users log in to an app called “This Is Your Digital Life” which asked questions and built profiles of the users. The data was then used for political campaigns, without users’ consent, including Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign.
The case in New Mexico alleged that Meta knew about third parties collecting the data and lied to Facebook users about it. The state also said that the company allowed hate speech and misinformation to spread on the social media site when it benefited the company, regardless of how it impacted users.
“The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook’s repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act,” Judge Francis Mathew wrote in a court filing after the verdict.
According to a report from Reuter’s, jurors found that Facebook “had committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws, based on the number of Facebook users or New Mexico residents who were the audience for each misleading statement.”
Judge Mathew found that the violations warranted a $219 billion penalty, but brought that number down to $25 billion. Meta asked that it be capped at $3.45 billion.
Meta’s chief legal officer, C.J. Mahoney released a statement following the judgement, saying that the company will appeal.
“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Mahoney said. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.”
Earlier this year, Meta was ordered to pay $375 million in a separate civil case, after a New Mexico court found that the company violated state consumer protection law by misleading users about the safety of its platforms for children.

sources.news_title: Meta ordered to cough up $25 billion in New Mexico privacy case
sources.text:
Meta ordered to cough up $25 billion in New Mexico privacy case
The case stemmed from the nearly decade-old Cambridge Analytica scandal.
If you thought Meta's self-inflicted blows from the Cambridge Analytica data harvesting scandal were over, think again. On Wednesday, a New Mexico judge ordered the company to pay the state $25 billion in penalties, having found that the company made misleading statements about the privacy of consumers in the state. "It has been a long time coming holding Big Tech accountable," New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a press conference (via Reuters).
The case, filed in 2021, wasn't directly about the data harvested by Cambridge Analytica. Instead, it targeted Facebook's statements over the years regarding user data, privacy settings and content moderation.
In September, a Santa Fe jury found that Meta violated New Mexico's Unfair Practices Act by misleading residents on those issues. The jury counted a staggering 43 million violations. At up to $5,000 for each violation, the maximum penalty came to about $219 billion.
The state asked for $35 billion to $40 billion, with New Mexico attorney Randi McGinn saying the court "should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the value of its stock price." Meta requested no more than $3.45 billion. Judge Francis Mathew ended up at $25 billion. He didn't hold back in his ruling, describing Facebook's promised post-scandal investigation as "willfully ineffective" while noting "the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements."
This lawsuit is separate from one the company recently settled with nearly every other US state over child safety concerns. That included nearly $459 million specifically for Cambridge Analytica data harvesting claims. New Mexico skipped that settlement, which opened the door to this trial.
The money will go to New Mexico's school system, with interest accruing at 15 percent a year until the penalty is paid in full. Meta has said it will appeal, with chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney calling it "a tax on speech."

sources.news_title: Meta to pay $25B in New Mexico case over misleading Facebook users
sources.text:
A New Mexico judge has ordered Meta to pay a $25B civil penalty for misleading Facebook users about their privacy and its hate speech rules, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday. It is among the largest verdicts in US legal history.
In September, a Santa Fe jury found Meta liable for more than 43 million violations of the state’s consumer protection law.
The case grew out of the Cambridge Analytica scandal, in which a political consulting firm got data on up to 87 million Facebook users.
The state also argued that some high-profile accounts got lighter scrutiny than ordinary users under Meta’s hate speech rules.
Judge Francis Mathew applied the maximum penalty of $5,000 per violation, which would have added up to $219B. He then cut it to $25B.
The state had asked for $35B to $40B, while Meta’s lawyers argued for no more than $3.4B, the Associated Press reported.
“Facebook’s wrongdoing, over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public, goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Mathew wrote.
Meta plans to appeal, the AP reported. Its lawyers had said a penalty in the tens of billions would be a “constitutional violation of epic proportions.”
They also argued the jury never found that anyone in New Mexico saw the statements or was harmed.
Attorney General Raúl Torrez, who filed the case in 2021, called the penalty “one of the single largest, if not the largest, single-state verdicts against a company in American history.”
He has said the money will go to a state education fund.
The sum exceeds the $14.8B in general-fund revenue New Mexico expects in fiscal 2028. It also tops the roughly $18B Meta agreed in August to pay most US states over harm to young users.
New Mexico stayed out of those group deals and went to court alone, even after Meta warned it could leave the state over its child safety demands.
It already won $375M from Meta in a child safety trial in March, plus a court order requiring it to pay $567M into a teen health fund.
Meta has paid before over Cambridge Analytica. It paid the Federal Trade Commission a $5B fine in 2019 and $725M to end a class action in 2022.

sources.news_title: Judge Orders Meta To Pay Blue State Billions, Empowers Democrat To Reinstate Censorship Regime
sources.text:
A New Mexico judge is ordering Meta to pay a massive $25 billion in penalties on Wednesday, an order that may empower the state’s far-Left attorney general to force the platform to reinstate censorship tools that it did away with after the 2024 election.
The case initially targeted Meta, the parent company of Facebook, over a data breach involving political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica, but the scope was broadened by Attorney General Raúl Torrez to criticize the social media giant’s content moderation strategy, The Daily Wire reported earlier this month.
The New Mexico district court judge Francis J. Mathew ultimately sided with Torrez and mentioned Facebook’s content moderation shortcomings in his ruling. The company was facing potential penalties of roughly $219 billion, nearly $20 billion more than the company’s total revenue from last year. Mathew later reduced the penalty to $25 billion—an amount still more than twice New Mexico’s state budget.
Meta argued Wednesday’s ruling makes it impossible for the company to do business in the state, signaling its belief that the ultimate goal was to institute “new rules for what people can say online.”
“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Meta attorney C.J. Mahoney said in a statement. “At its core this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.”
Lawyer Jordan Sekulow echoes the sentiment, saying the massive financial penalty was an attempt to pressure Facebook back into censorship.
“New Mexico’s Attorney General should not dictate what Americans can say online or use massive financial penalties to pressure companies into censorship,” Sekulow said.
During the trial, as was first reported by The Daily Wire, Torrez made clear he did not approve of Meta switching its content moderation strategy from internal fact-checkers to a “community notes” system. Torrez claimed the company “bragged about” its fact checking strategy but abandoned it after Trump won the 2024 presidential election.
“When Donald Trump wins the presidency again a second time … Facebook announces we’re getting rid of their fact-check program, and we’re just going to switch to what everybody else has — the community notes program,” he complained during the trial.

sources.text:
A New Mexico state judge today ordered Meta Platforms to pay $25 billion after a Santa Fe jury found in September that the company misled the public about privacy on Facebook, according to reports by the Associated Press and Reuters. Judge Francis Mathew wrote that a penalty of more than $219 billion was warranted under state law before reducing the figure, according to Reuters.
In Short
A judge in New Mexico told Meta to pay $25 billion because a jury decided the company had said misleading things about how it handles Facebook users' data, mostly in the years around the Cambridge Analytica scandal. The money is supposed to go to New Mexico's schools, but Meta is expected to appeal, so nothing will be paid soon. The case shows a single state can count every resident who saw a company's public privacy promises as a separate violation, and that math turned a privacy case into one of the largest state penalties ever reported.
The order and the numbers
The penalty was handed down on Wednesday, October 21, 2026. Both news reports date the order to that day: the Associated Press story, by Mikella Schuettler of the AP/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative and published by ABC News, says "a judge on Wednesday ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion," and the Reuters report by Diana Novak Jones says the order came "on Wednesday" as well. The jury's verdict is older. Reuters dates it to September 25, while the AP report says only that it came in September.
What separates the two numbers in the Reuters account is the most striking detail of the day. "Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219 billion was warranted, based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion," according to Reuters. The AP report does not mention the $219 billion figure.
That ceiling follows from the arithmetic of the statute. According to Reuters, "State law allows a penalty of up to $5,000 per violation," and jurors found more than 43 million violations. PPC Land's coverage of the September verdict reported the exact figure on the verdict form as 43,899,720 violations, with a theoretical maximum of about $219.5 billion. On PPC Land's own calculation, $25 billion spread across 43,899,720 violations works out to about $569 per violation, or roughly 11.4% of the statutory ceiling.
The parties had argued for very different numbers. According to the AP report, "Attorneys for New Mexico had sought $35 billion to $40 billion, arguing that the company would only change its ways with a sum that affected its stock price." Reuters places that request at a hearing on October 1, where Randi McGinn, a lawyer for the state, asked for the same range. "This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the value of its stock price," McGinn said, according to Reuters.
Meta asked for far less. The AP report says lawyers for the company "argued for paying no more than $3.4 billion." Reuters puts Meta's proposed cap at $3.45 billion. By PPC Land's calculation, the state's range equals roughly $797 to $911 per violation, and Meta's $3.45 billion figure about $79.
In his written order, Mathew framed the conduct in broad terms. "Facebook's wrongdoing - over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public - goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices," the judge wrote, according to Reuters. Neither report quotes any other passage of the order, and neither says whether the order includes injunctive terms.
Where the money goes
Both outlets say the money is earmarked for education, though they describe the legal basis differently. "Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violations of consumer protection laws go state education spending," according to the AP report. Reuters attributes the destination to state law and to New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez, who said the law "directs that all of the money go to New Mexico's school system," as Reuters paraphrased his remarks after the verdict.
Torrez acknowledged the timing problem. "We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years," he said, according to the AP report, which adds that Torrez "acknowledged that the money would be tied up if Meta appeals as expected."
Torrez's claim about scale
The attorney general's description of the award differs slightly between the two reports. The AP quotes Torrez as calling it "one of the largest, if not the single largest state verdict against a company in American history." Reuters paraphrases him as saying it was "one of the largest, if not the largest, single state verdict against the company in American history" - against Meta specifically, rather than any company. Neither outlet independently checks the claim.
At a press conference in Albuquerque after the ruling, Torrez spoke more broadly. "It has been a long time coming holding Big Tech accountable," he said, according to Reuters. "I think today's judgment is a clear break with that past and a very clear warning to those in this space and beyond that we intend to protect our people and protect our consumers." The AP report carries a different line from the same day: "This judgement should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley."
What the jury decided in September
The case was tried on statements, not on the data harvest itself. According to Reuters, "Jurors on September 25 found that 26 of 29 statements made by the company and its leadership on those issues were misleading." The violation count was built "based on the number of Facebook users or New Mexico residents who were the audience for each misleading statement," Reuters reported.
The AP report describes the jury's work differently. "During the trial, jurors assessed whether Facebook misled users about privacy and content moderation 34 separate times," it says. It does not explain how 34 assessments relate to the 29 statements Reuters describes, and the two reports cannot be reconciled from their own text. PPC Land's September coverage noted that the verdict form was divided into five parts and that one statement was examined twice, which accounts for some but not all of the gap.
On the scale of the count, the AP report says jurors agreed with the state's premise that Facebook's statements "deceived the entire population of New Mexico and extended beyond social media users," and "found Facebook liable for 2.1 million violations on certain counts, bringing the total number of violations to over 43 million." That 2.1 million figure matches PPC Land's reading of the verdict form, where jurors assigned 2,100,000 violations to each of 11 statements distributed through major news outlets and 1,386,648 to each of 15 published on Facebook's own channels.
The defence did win on one point. "In one of the few wins for the defense, jurors found the state didn't prove that Facebook made false claims about removing harmful content, including misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic," according to the AP report.
Which law, which court
Neither news report names the statute. The AP report refers to "New Mexico consumer protection laws" and Reuters to "New Mexico's consumer protection laws." PPC Land's reporting from the verdict identified the claims as brought under New Mexico's Unfair Practices Act in the First Judicial District Court for Santa Fe County, case D-101-CV-2021-00132. Reuters says only that it was "a Santa Fe jury," and both outlets name Francis Mathew as the judge.
The precise legal form of today's decision is also left loose. The AP calls it an order, a "judgement" in Torrez's quote and a "penalty announcement" when describing the share price; Reuters uses "order," "ruling" and "judgment." Neither says whether a final judgment has been entered, which matters for when appeal deadlines begin to run.
The data practices at issue
For advertisers, the substance of the case lies in what the state said Facebook told the public about data. According to Reuters, "The state accused Meta of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data, how the company handles hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform and other internal policies." Reuters adds that, in the state's account, "the company knew that third parties had broad access to users' personal data, and it tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company's bottom line."
The AP report centres the privacy claims on Cambridge Analytica. "The state's case focused on accusations that Facebook deceived users about a data breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, to generate targeted ads," according to the AP. "The now-defunct firm's clients included the 2016 campaign for President Donald Trump."
Reuters gives the same scale with more hedging - "as many as 87 million Facebook users" - and explains the mechanism. Cambridge Analytica "gained access to the personal information from millions of Facebook accounts for the purposes of voter profiling and targeting," according to Reuters, and "obtained that information without users' consent from a researcher who had been allowed by Facebook to deploy an app on its social media network that harvested data from millions of its users."
The two outlets describe the transfer slightly differently. The AP says the quiz data was "sold" to Cambridge Analytica. Reuters says the firm "obtained" the data from the researcher and does not say whether money changed hands.
Meta's defence on data went to the core of its ad model. According to Reuters, "The evidence showed that Meta does not sell user data and New Mexico did not prove that any consumer had actually been misled, the company said in court filings." That position echoes one of the statements on trial: PPC Land reported that the statements at issue included a 2019 remark by Sheryl Sandberg that Facebook does not sell user data or tell advertisers who users are. Neither of today's reports says how the jury treated that particular statement.
Content moderation claims
The privacy claims sat alongside allegations about content. "New Mexico prosecutors also argued that Facebook allowed misinformation or violent content to proliferate on the platform," according to the AP report. "Defense attorneys vehemently denied the allegations, saying the company's content moderation policies are robust and freedom of speech has to be considered."
McGinn told jurors in her closing argument that Facebook profited from harmful content, "which CEO Mark Zuckerberg denied during his video deposition," according to the AP. Zuckerberg said the company has to balance freedom of speech with content moderation, the AP reported. Facebook's lawyers said the company had adapted its policies since the suit was filed in 2021 and "that it removes 99% of content that violates standards," according to the same report.
Meta's arguments and the appeal
Meta did not comment on the amount in either report. "Representatives for Meta, which previously said it plans to appeal the September verdict, didn't immediately respond to a message seeking comment about the amount," according to the AP. Reuters reported that "a spokesperson for Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment." After the verdict in September, Meta spokesperson Alex Burgos said the company disagreed with the verdict and would continue to defend itself.
The company's case for a lower number rested on constitutional limits. According to the AP, Meta's lawyers said an award ten times $3.4 billion "or even more would violate due process, was unconstitutional and would not hold up under appeal." Meta attorney Matt Nicholson argued in court that a sum as high as $40 billion would be "shocking to the conscience," the AP reported. Reuters adds an economic argument: Meta said in filings that a higher penalty "ran the risk of scaring businesses out of the state."
The most likely target on appeal is the violation count itself. "The jury didn't make findings that any New Mexican heard or saw these statements, or was harmed by them," Nicholson said at the October 1 hearing, according to the AP. The AP reports that Meta's lawyers called it "unprecedented for the state to count the number of violations based on how many individuals may have heard or seen the misleading statements from the company, arguing there was no evidence these statements ever harmed anyone." In later filings, Facebook's attorneys argued the state's consumer protection laws "don't apply to people in New Mexico who weren't using the platform at the time," the AP said.
Per-violation penalties of this kind work much like statutory damages: the law fixes a sum for each violation, and no individual loss has to be proven. That is why the method of counting matters more than the cap. According to the AP, "In appealing the jury's verdict, Meta might reduce the number of violations and therefore the total financial penalty," while "interest on the penalty would accrue during an appeal."
During closing arguments, Facebook's lawyers also said the state's evidence was outdated "and that despite having five years to gather material, New Mexico found only one other instance of a data breach," according to the AP.
Injunction still open
According to the AP, "The state is also seeking an injunction to stop similar practices." Reuters does not mention an injunction. Neither report says whether Mathew has ruled on it, so the business-practice consequences of the case remain unclear.
The market reaction
Investors did not treat the number as a threat. The AP reported that Meta "was scheduled to report its quarterly earnings Wednesday afternoon and its shares were trading 2% higher following the penalty announcement." Reuters quoted Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson & Co, who called the ruling costly. "Having said that, Meta is worth nearly two trillion dollars, and will likely continue to appeal these cases and drag them out," Luria said. "That means the current set of cases is unlikely to cause a material impact to Meta's value."
The August settlement and why New Mexico went to trial
This is where the two reports diverge most sharply. According to the AP, "New Mexico was the only state to pursue a trial around the Cambridge Analytica scandal after 48 other states signed a settlement for $18 billion in August." The AP adds that "besides New Mexico, Florida was the only other state that did not sign the settlement, which included an agreement to release Meta from future liability related to the Cambridge Analytica privacy breach." Earlier in the same story, the AP says "Forty-eight other states settled with Facebook in a nationwide case."
Reuters describes a different structure. "The ruling comes after six other states settled their lawsuits related to Cambridge Analytica, the consulting firm, for $459.2 million as part of a $17.1 billion multistate settlement Meta reached in August to resolve states' claims that the company's platforms had harmed teen mental health," according to Reuters.
So the AP frames the August deal as an $18 billion Cambridge Analytica settlement signed by 48 states, while Reuters frames it as a $17.1 billion teen mental health settlement that folded in $459.2 million for six states' Cambridge Analytica claims. PPC Land's own reading of the agreement supports the Reuters structure and explains the competing totals. The consent judgment signed in Oakland on August 26 described a separate $459.29 million "Cambridge Settlement Amount" resolving four "Cambridge Complaints," while New Jersey's announcement cited up to $17.1 billion and Meta's own post cited about $18 billion. That agreement covered 51 jurisdictions, according to PPC Land. Neither news report explains why New Mexico stayed out, beyond the AP's note that the state "chose to take the social media company to court on its own."
Earlier settlements tied to the same events are part of the background. In March 2026, a San Francisco court entered a $50 million judgment against Meta in California's case over Facebook user data shared with third-party developers, conduct a deputy attorney general said "arose from the circumstances giving rise to the Cambridge Analytica scandal." In November 2025, Meta agreed to pay $190 million to settle a shareholder derivative suit over privacy failures linked to Cambridge Analytica. That suit traced back to the FTC's $5 billion penalty and the 20-year consent decree stipulated on July 24, 2019. The Reuters page also links to its December 2022 report on a $725 million settlement of a lawsuit relating to Cambridge Analytica, though the article text does not discuss it.
A second Santa Fe loss in six months
Today's order is the second large monetary outcome for New Mexico against Meta this year. "The verdict was the second in six months by a Santa Fe jury in a lawsuit brought by the state of New Mexico against Meta Platforms," according to Reuters.
In the first trial, which ended in March, "a Santa Fe jury found Meta misled users about young users' safety on its Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp platforms and ordered the company to pay $375 million in civil penalties," Reuters reported. PPC Land covered that March 24 verdict and the $375 million penalty at the time. "After a second phase of that trial, a judge directed the company to pay $567 million into a New Mexico fund for teen mental health and ordered Meta to implement measures to protect teen Facebook and Instagram users in New Mexico," according to Reuters. That August 6 abatement order was issued by a different judge, Chief District Court Judge Bryan Biedscheid, and included a monthly cap of 90 hours of use for under-18 accounts in the state, according to PPC Land.
PPC Land reported in September that Meta had not paid the $375 million March penalty and had posted a $1.8 billion bond while appealing earlier judgments. If the pattern holds, today's $25 billion order will follow the same route through the appellate courts, with interest building in the meantime.
Why it matters for marketers
Meta's advertising business depends on users trusting the platform with data that is then used for targeting - a point the company's own executives addressed in some of the very statements jurors found misleading. Cambridge Analytica built political ad audiences from Facebook data, and the AP described the purpose plainly: the harvested data was used "to generate targeted ads."
Three features of the case reach beyond Meta. First, the penalty was calculated per audience member, not per affected user or per dollar of harm, and both news reports describe that method as the central dispute. If it survives appeal, public statements about data handling - in press interviews, blog posts and executive remarks - carry a liability that scales with reach. Second, the case shows how a single state can reject a multistate deal and pursue a far larger outcome at trial: on Reuters' figures, the $25 billion order is more than 50 times the $459.2 million six states accepted for their Cambridge Analytica claims, by PPC Land's calculation. Third, the judge's own reading of the law put the ceiling at more than $219 billion, which leaves room for a higher number if the count is challenged and the penalty is revisited.
What neither report establishes is just as relevant. Neither quotes the order beyond one sentence, neither says whether injunctive terms were granted, and the outlets disagree on the size and structure of the August settlement. The appellate path, and the court's treatment of the per-resident counting method, will determine how much of today's figure Meta pays.

sources.text:
Meta ordered to pay $25 billion in Cambridge Analytica case
October 21, 2026
US tech giant Meta, owner of Facebook, was ordered to pay $25 billion (around €22.5 billion) to the US state of New Mexico after a jury found Facebook deceived its users over privacy and content moderation.
"Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the Wednesday verdict.
The case links back to the 2016 Cambridge Analytica scandal, when a third-party quiz harvested the data of some 87 million Facebook profiles and sold it to the UK-based political consulting firm. The firm used the data for targeted ads, including campaign ads for Donald Trump's first presidential run.
New Mexico rejects deal with Meta
Nearly all US states agreed to settle with Facebook over a myriad of legal issues for an overall payment of $18 billion in August. This included releasing the company from future liability for the Cambridge Analytica breach.
New Mexico refused to settle and filed a lawsuit against the platform. Prosecutors claimed that the social network deceived the state's entire population of some 2.1 million people by its public statements on privacy. The US state also argued that Facebook allowed the spread of misinformation and violent content.
In turn, the company's lawyers said the state failed to prove people were actually harmed by Facebook's statements, and claimed the platform had robust content moderation.
In September, a jury found Facebook liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws. Meta pledged to "continue to defend ourselves against efforts to distort our record."
Meta's billions could go to New Mexico's education system
Following the jury's decision last month, it was up to the court to determine how much Meta would pay the state. While the $25 billion fine is lower than the $35 billion to $40 billion demanded by the New Mexico prosecutors, it far exceeds the cap of $3.45 billion suggested by Meta's lawyers.
"This court should speak to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the value of its stock price," New Mexico attorney Randi McGinn said during the trial.
On Wednesday, New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez said the outcome should be "an unambiguous message" to Silicon Valley.
While noting that the money will likely be tied up due to appeals, Torrez also noted that the fine is legally due to be paid into New Mexico's education fund.
"We may have paid for the construction of schools for the next 100 years," he said.
The case is the latest in the string of legal challenges large social media companies face in the US and other parts of the world, including the separate August verdict in New Mexico ordering Facebook to pay $567 million over harm to children.

sources.news_title: New Mexico judge orders Meta to pay state $25B
sources.text:
New Mexico judge orders Meta to pay state $25B
New Mexico First Judicial District Judge Francis Mathew listens to attorney Matthew Nicholson, representing Meta Platforms Inc., during an Oct. 1, 2026, hearing to determine the penalties against Meta. Mathew issued that ruling on Oct. 21, 2026, fining the company $25 billion. (Eddie Moore/Albuquerque Journal)
A New Mexico District judge on Wednesday ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties for violating state law regarding unfair and deceptive trade practices.
The state was entitled to closer to $220 billion, First Judicial District Judge Francis Mathew wrote, although the company will accrue 15% in interest annually until it pays off the penalty.
The decision follows a Santa Fe jury’s finding in late September that Facebook, which is owned by Meta, committed close to 44 million violations of New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act.
“This is a historic day for New Mexico and for consumers across the country,” Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a statement following Mathew’s ruling. “We took on one of the largest companies in the world because New Mexicans deserve honesty, accountability, and the protection of their personal information. Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable.”
In five separate categories, the jury found that Facebook misrepresented or made false statements regarding users’ ability to control their data; the company’s own efforts to combat hate speech and misinformation; its application of community standards uniformly; and its commitment to conduct a thorough investigation after the Cambridge Analytica scandal broke. In total, the jury sided with the state on 31 out of 34 counts, according to the jury verdict form.
Attorneys for New Mexico’s Department of Justice had requested up to $40 billion in penalties, though the state was entitled to up to $5,000 per violation.
In fact, Mathew wrote in his decision that “the extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of the New Mexico audiences reached, and the clearly intentional and systematic nature of Facebook’s repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty.”
Torrez, at a Wednesday news conference, told reporters that the multibillion-dollar judgment was a clear sign of what New Mexico is capable of by going it alone in court. The $25 billion is larger than settlements delivered in high-profile multi-state lawsuits that settled earlier this year.
“I think today’s judgment from a state which admittedly is not very big in terms of population should be a clear warning to everyone in big tech,” Torrez said.
Mathew’s decision not to award the full $219.5 billion judgment “shouldn’t be mistaken for the larger message, which is this…one of the largest, if not the largest, state-led recoveries and jury verdicts in American history.”
The New Mexico Department of Justice brought the suit under the state’s consumer protection law, the Unfair Practices Act. Torrez and a state lawmaker recently announced their plans to revamp the decades-old law, which caps penalties at $5,000 per violation, in the upcoming legislative session.
“While I am extraordinarily proud of the fact that we achieved this outcome using a law that came into effect before I was born, I think it is very clear that that’s a law that needs to be dramatically restructured,” he told reporters. “The Unfair Practices Act was designed for an era that frankly doesn’t exist anymore.”
One of the attorneys who represented the state, Randi McGinn from the McGinn Montoya Love Curry and Sievers law firm, issued a statement that said the court “spoke to Meta in the only language it understands, which is money, and the value of its stock price.” Her statement also noted that with the ruling, Meta “learned that lying to New Mexicans has a price. I’m grateful to our Attorney General Raul Torrez for letting a New Mexico jury of ordinary citizens stand up for truth against one of the largest social media companies in the world.”
New Mexico House Democrats also issued statements praising Torrez and the ruling, with state Rep. Nathan Small (D-Las Cruces), who chairs the Legislative Finance Council and the House Appropriations and Finance Committee issuing a statement that the money would be put to good use: “As we build our state budgets for the years to come,” he said, “We will make sure these dollars are directed to protecting New Mexicans that have been harmed, and most importantly to protecting and engaging our kids who are navigating an unprecedented world.”
Torrez, during the conference, said he expects Meta to appeal.
Indeed, a statement provided to Source NM from C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said: “This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico. At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal. In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge.”

sources.news_title: Meta ordered to pay New Mexico $25 billion for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook - The Boston Globe
sources.text:
A judge on Wednesday ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant.
Facebook’s conduct was intentional and executives consistently misled users about how the platform worked, state District Court Judge Francis J. Mathew wrote in his ruling.
“Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false,” he said.
State Attorney General Raúl Torrez said at a news conference that the award should be seen as a warning to tech companies that New Mexico will hold them accountable.
“This judgment should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley,” he said.
Representatives for Meta, which previously said it plans to appeal the September verdict, didn’t immediately respond to a message seeking comment about the amount. The Menlo Park, California-based company was scheduled to report its quarterly earnings Wednesday afternoon and its shares were trading 2 percent higher following the penalty announcement.
New Mexico goes it alone
In August, Meta reached a settlement with nearly all states and territories — except New Mexico and Florida — to pay $18 billion and add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms.
The settlement ended a trial over teen social media addiction and resolved a pivotal case years in the making that sought to hold the tech giant accountable for the role its platforms played in undermining children’s mental health. The effort targeted features designed to grab young people’s attention.
New Mexico wasn’t part of the multistate settlement because it was pursuing its own case.
Jurors in September found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws when a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, harvested Facebook user data to generate targeted political ads for the 2016 election.
Attorneys for New Mexico had sought $35 billion to $40 billion, arguing that the company would only change its ways with a sum that affected its stock price.
Lawyers for Meta argued for paying no more than $3.4 billion. An award 10 times that or even more would violate due process, was unconstitutional and would not hold up under appeal, they said.
Meta argued the state failed to prove misleading statements about privacy and that content moderation actually harmed New Mexicans. Interest on the penalty would accrue during an appeal, but the number of violations Meta is charged with could be reduced.
Meta attorney Matt Nicholson argued in court that a sum as high as $40 billion would be “shocking to the conscience” while an attorney for New Mexico, Randi McGinn, urged standing up to “tech titans who think they are bulletproof and can do whatever they want.”
The amount awarded in the case far exceeds the $5 billion fine that the Federal Trade Commission levied against Facebook in 2019.
Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violations of consumer protection laws go toward state education spending. Torrez acknowledged the money would be tied up as Meta appeals.
Company argues that the state failed to prove harm
The state’s case focused on accusations that Facebook deceived users about a data breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to a political consulting firm, Cambridge Analytica, to generate targeted ads. The now-defunct firm’s clients included the 2016 campaign for President Donald Trump.
Attorneys for New Mexico argued that the state’s entire population, not just Facebook users, were deceived by the company’s public statements about privacy on the platform. Facebook’s lawyers argued that the state failed to prove whether people were actually harmed by these deceiving statements.
“The jury didn’t make findings that any New Mexican heard or saw these statements, or was harmed by them,” said Nicholson during a hearing Oct. 1.
New Mexico prosecutors also argued that Facebook allowed misinformation or violent content to proliferate on the platform. Defense attorneys vehemently denied the allegations, saying the company’s content moderation policies are robust and freedom of speech has to be considered.
Jury finds millions of violations
New Mexico was the only state to pursue a trial around the Cambridge Analytica scandal after 48 other states signed a settlement for $18 billion in August.
Besides New Mexico, Florida was the only other state that did not sign the settlement, which included an agreement to release Meta from future liability related to the Cambridge Analytica privacy breach.
During the trial, jurors assessed whether Facebook misled users about privacy and content moderation 34 separate times. State prosecutors, though, argued Facebook’s statements deceived the entire population of New Mexico and extended beyond social media users.
In the end, jurors agreed with this premise and found Facebook liable for 2.1 million violations on certain counts, bringing the total number of violations to over 43 million.
Facebook’s attorneys have argued in subsequent court filings that the state’s consumer protection laws don’t apply to people in New Mexico who weren’t using the platform at the time.
Torrez told reporters following the verdict that all money awarded will go into a fund for the state’s education system. The state is also seeking an injunction to stop similar practices.
Meta questions evidence and tally of violations
In appealing the jury’s verdict, Meta might reduce the number of violations and therefore the total financial penalty. Lawyers for the company said it was unprecedented for the state to count the number of violations based on how many individuals may have heard or seen the misleading statements from the company, arguing there was no evidence these statements ever harmed anyone.
During closing arguments, lawyers for Facebook said the state’s evidence was outdated and that despite having five years to gather material, New Mexico found only one other instance of a data breach.
In one of the few wins for the defense, jurors found the state didn’t prove that Facebook made false claims about removing harmful content, including misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic.
The state said the company favored certain accounts and allowed for violent or inaccurate content to proliferate. Attorney Randi McGinn said in her closing argument for the state that Facebook profited off harmful content, which CEO Mark Zuckerberg denied during his video deposition. Zuckerberg said the company has to carefully balance freedom of speech with content moderation.
Attorneys for Facebook said the company has adapted its policies since the state’s lawsuit was filed in 2021 and that it removes 99 percent of content that violates standards.
In a previous version of this story, the Associated Press misspelled the judge’s name.
Associated Press reporter Matthew Brown and Technology Writer Barbara Ortutay contributed to this report.

sources.text:
The Cambridge Analytica scandal has come back to haunt Meta after a New Mexico judge ordered it to pay $25 billion in penalties for more than 43 million violations of the state’s unfair practices law. The ruling marks the biggest legal hit Meta has taken this year, even as it’s faced several other losses or settlements.
Meta ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties over the Cambridge Analytica scandal
It’s significantly more than it agreed to pay in a recent kids online safety settlement.
A New Mexico jury ruled in September that Meta misled consumers over how it protected their data and prevented misinformation and hate speech on its platforms. The case stemmed from a 2021 complaint in the wake of the revelations a few years earlier that UK political consultancy Cambridge Analytica harvested data from millions of Facebook accounts to pinpoint messages that would resonate with voters leading up to President Donald Trump’s first election. The judge found that the “extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership,” and other factors justified the highest penalty allowed under the law, at $5,000 per violation. That brings the total civil penalties to more than $219 billion, but the judge reduced it to $25 billion.
“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Meta’s chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal.”
“New Mexico stood its ground”
Even this smaller sum is “one of the largest financial penalties against a corporation in U.S. history,” according to the AG’s office, and dwarfs other recent rulings and settlements involving Meta. In another landmark ruling in New Mexico state court, Meta was ordered to pay a total of nearly $1 billion in civil penalties and abatement for misleading the public about the safety of its products. In a separate agreement with most other state AGs, Meta settled an array of kids online safety complaints for $17.1 billion — but $5.3 billion of that is contingent on YouTube and TikTok installing similar measures.
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez issued a triumphant statement after the latest in his string of wins against Meta (though the company managed to fight off many of the business changes the AG asked for in the remedies portion of the kids online safety case). “This case has always been about more than one company or one scandal,” Torrez said. “It is about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences. New Mexico stood its ground, took this case to trial, and secured a verdict establishing millions of violations of our law.”

No merger agreement or exchange terms have been announced. A combination would bring very different businesses and their shareholders under one corporate roof, following SpaceX’s absorption of Mr. Musk’s artificial-intelligence company xAI.

sources.news_title: Meta fined $US25 billion over New Mexico data privacy
sources.text:
Meta fined $US25 billion over New Mexico data privacy
|
A judge in New Mexico has ordered Meta to pay $US25 billion after a jury found the tech giant had misled consumers in a case arising from allegations that a political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their consent.
New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez said it was one of the largest, if not the largest, single state verdict against a company in American history.
“Facebook’s wrongdoing – over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public – goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the verdict.
Mathew found that a penalty of more than $US219 billion was warranted, based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion.
In a statement, C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal.
“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Mahoney said.
“At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.”
The company had previously said a penalty in the billions of dollars risked violating its constitutional rights to due process and protection from excessive fines.
The penalty is the largest levied against the tech giant in the wake of the Cambridge Analytica scandal. In 2019, the company was hit with a $US5 billion penalty by the US Federal Trade Commission stemming from the same scandal.
Six other states settled their lawsuits related to Cambridge Analytica for $459.2 million as part of a $17.1 billion multistate settlement Meta reached in August to resolve states’ claims that the company’s platforms had harmed teen mental health.
New Mexico’s attorney general had sued Meta in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app.
The state accused Meta of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data, how the company handles hate speech and misinformation posted on the platform and other internal policies.
The company knew that third parties had broad access to users’ personal data, and it tolerated hate speech or other harmful content when it benefited the company’s bottom line, the state said.
Cambridge Analytica, now defunct, worked for Trump’s successful presidential campaign in 2016, and gained access to the personal information from millions of Facebook accounts for the purposes of voter profiling and targeting. It obtained that information without users’ consent from a researcher who had been allowed by Facebook to deploy an app on its social media network.
“It has been a long time coming holding Big Tech accountable,” Torrez told a press conference in Albuquerque after the ruling.
“I think today’s judgment is a clear break with that past and a very clear warning to those in this space and beyond that we intend to protect our people and protect our consumers.”
Analyst Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson & Co, called the ruling costly but unlikely to impact the company’s value.
“Meta is worth nearly two trillion dollars, and will likely continue to appeal these cases and drag them out,” Luria said.
In court filings, Meta urged Mathew to cap the penalties at $US3.45 billion, saying a higher penalty ran the risk of scaring businesses out of the state. The evidence showed that Meta does not sell user data and New Mexico did not prove that any consumer had actually been misled, the company said in court filings.
The verdict was the second in six months by a Santa Fe jury in a lawsuit brought by the state of New Mexico against Meta Platforms.
Reuters
